I would like to direct the attention of the House to a matter which occurred on 6th March when the estimates of the Defence department were before the committee. I asked a question with reference to an item and was told that the information I desired was contained in Hansard of last year. I sent to my room for the bound copy of Hansard which had been supplied to me. Afterwards I made further reference to the matter, but was informed by the chairman of the committee that I was out of order in doing so. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) asked me a question, and, instead of answering him, I sent across the floor of the House the bound volume which I had obtained. He is reported in Hansard to have said:
In the copy of Hansard which ray hon. friend has just handed me it looks as though those pages had been cut out.
I did not take notice of it at the time, but I have observed since that several references have been made to it in the press, and the impression is being given, or the insinuation made, that some person was a party to cutting these leaves out of Hansard. I called up Mr. Cook, who, I thought, was still connected with the Bureau. A few days ago I handed him the volume and he took it to the Librarian of Parliament. I interviewed the librarian, and from him I have obtained the following statement which, with your permission and the consent of the House, I would like to have placed on Hansard:
Ottawa, 8th March, 1923. Donald Sutherland, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear sirI beg to confirm what I mentioned to you this morning: Mr. Fred Cook brought to the library, this morning, a copy of the House of Commons Hansard, vol. 3, 1922, out of which after page 2082, a whole signature was missing. Being asked if there was any trace of this signature having been either torn from the book or otherwise separated from it, I carefully examined the appearance of the volume, and found no sign of cut thread, or remnant of the sewing thread. I concluded and answ-ered that this was evidently a case of the gatherer at the printing bureau having omitted to insert the missing signature in its proper place, or having wrongly placed it elsewhere. I brought the volume to our expert binder, Mr. Brown, and asked him what he thought of the appearance, and he fully confirmed my impression.
Yours very truly,
J. de L. Tache,
.	General Librarian.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Immigration is probably one of the most discussed subjects in Canada, and in a brief way I hope this afternoon to cover some of the important points, at least so far as I am able to see them, and the recommendations that have been made to the government with respect to this very important matter. .

I think, Mr. Chairman, that one can best begin a discussion of this subject by giving a review of opinion in our own country. I have heard a great many different views expressed during the past summer with respect to this question. Some people are of the opinion that we should take steps to bring a huge tide of immigration to Canada; and not only that, but that we should follow some method such as that adopted for the settlement of our returned soldiers,-borrowing large sums of money for the purpose of settling upon our vacant lands people who Will come to us from the various parts of the world. Others oppose that idea, and many Canadian agriculturists feel-and they have so expressed their feeling to me-that it is our first business to make the people already on the land prosperous before bringing more upon the land and placing them in a. similar condition.
I want to take the middle course between the two extremes. I think I may preface my remarks by saying that with the problem that Canada has to face, with the financial obligations that the people of Canada now have to shoulder, it is imperative that we get more people to assist with this burden that is bearing rather heavily upon our shoulders to-day. Sometimes, one cannot help comparing today's conditions with those of eight, ten or fifteen years ago when we had, perhaps not so large a flow of immigration, as is sometimes stated, but a flow annually that would be regarded as reasonable. While I adopt the middle position, I am not unmindful of the fact, as I said before, that it is imperative to add to the population Of Canada; but that addition should be made with care, with a view to the assimilation of the people who will come amongst us and the making of a Canadian citizenship that we shall be proud of. That leads one to this point, and I will not enlarge very greatly upon it. Having all these things in mind, what class of people can we take into Canada and absorb most readily to-day, and who are the most desirable people to come amongst us? After a survey of conditions in Canada, one is led to the conclusion that there is not a great need of immigrants in our cities, particularly in the larger centres. The records of the past year or two have shown that we have had unemployment and that additions to the urban population of very large numbers would create a situation that would not be well for Canada. Not only that, but we must admit that for the past year or two, from the urban centres of Canada a very considerable number of people have left us and gone across the line to the United States. That

Supply-I mmigra tion
movement has been accelerated by the fact that the American government have seen fit to place in their Immigration Act a clause providing that from outside countries, with the exception of Canada, three per cent is the maximum number that will be permitted to land in the United States during any one calendar year. Canada alone is the exception ; from Canada immigrants may flow freely into the United States, and this has created in the United States, particularly in the urban centres, a scarcity of labour that is being supplied from the urban centres of Canada, and to some extent from our rural sections as well.
Let me say, in passing, that I doubt if we shall ever reach the time when we shall not have an efflux of Canadians into the United States. I have looked carefully over the records of the past fifteen years, and I find that it is somewhat surprising that during all those years there has been a fairly steady movement in that direction. The movement has varied a little, some years more some less, some years not quite counteracted by the movement from the United States to Canada; but during all those years that exodus seems to have kept up, and probably it will continue for some time. Therefore, we are restricted in the industrial field, particularly in the urban centres, although that is not quite so apparent to-day as it was three' months ago, and we are limited to the rural field for settlement of people whom we shall bring to Canada.
This brings me to the point where I wish to discuss for a few moments conditions as we find them in rural localities in Canada. I know that hon. gentlemen opposite will say that there are two or three outstanding reasons why agriculture is to-day in its present financial condition. Perhaps, the tariff has a great deal to do with the matter; perhaps a reason may be that transportation costs are high, or interest charges are unreaonable; and I am going to admit, in a reasonable way, because I do not want to be unreasonable, that many of these things are factors in producing present-day conditions, coupled with the sudden depression in prices of products of the farms of Canada and with no corresponding reduction in the price of commodities that the agriculturists must use in their business. But let us be fair. There are other influences that, perhaps have had some effect. Is it not a fact that inflated values as a result of the war-and I speak as one of those who are affected because I have no other business than that of agricuture and I know somewhat of those conditions-led us into difficulties in connection with purchasing land and with reaching out maybe a little further than we should have gone. I am not unmindful of the fact that some will say that we were encouraged to do so; that we were asked to produce in a way that we had never produced before in order that the world's supplies of food might be kept up to the necessities of that period. I am not unmindful of all those .things; but perhaps over-reaching has also contributed somewhat to the difficulties in which we find ourselves to-day. All these factors-and I have not time to deal with them now - have left agriculture, from one end of Canada to the other, in a somewhat depressed condition.
But again, I think we can get some encouragement by looking backward I know there are in this House to-day many hon. members who will remember that period of the early nineties. I was farming in Ontario at that time-and perhaps many here were engaged in the same occupation-and agricultural conditions then in my opinion, were worse than they are to-day in Canada. Looking back upon that period, I remember that wheat, cattle, hogs, dairy products were lower in price than they have been during the past two years. I will say this, that the commodities which we had to purchase in order to carry on our business were also 25 or 30 per cent lower, and in that respect, perhaps, the situation is almost evened up. We did not recover rapidly from that condition of affairs during that period. True, we did begin to recover in 1894, 1895 and 1896, and I suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) will tell me that the real era of prosperity began in 1896. Perhaps, our recovery in the present case will be found to have begun from the year 1921.
Pretty slow.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
On the old and well known ground, as I have just stated to the leader of the Opposition, that in countries such as Canada agriculture cannot long continue in a depressed state. I will admit to my hon. friend that there are conditions today to be met with that have not had to be faced in the past, conditions in connection with the various articles that go to make up cost, that have not had to be coped with in the past in the same manner as they will have to be met to-day. But there must come a levelling-up between the amount the farmer receives for his labour and that received by labour in other walks of life. That inevitably must come about. And just as sure as there is in the American states to-day an unprecedented era of prosperity in the urban communities, perhaps previously unknown in the history of that country, there is a corresponding depression in agriculture. I shall deal with that point for a moment or two this 
afternoon and recite some of my experiences in that connection. But let me observe in passing that I am not suggesting, as someone is sure to imply in a moment, that labour should take less for that which it is so frequently represented as selling. Someone is sure to ask, are they to take less?. I am not suggesting that. I am suggesting that labour will be enabled to purchase more of the necessities of life and that there will be a reduction in the natural commodities that pass between one class of the community and the other. I am not unmindful of conditions as they are, but with them I cannot at present deal for any considerable length of time. I will touch them again perhaps - a little more fully when I come to consider the question as to the class of people whom we hope to encourage to come to Canada.
Conditions to-day, however, are changing very rapidly in Canada; they change month by month. Three months ago we could not have held out encouragement to labourers to come to Canada to secure employment unless they were agricultural labourers; and I think that one of the problems that has to be faced to-day, in contrast with days gone by in connection with immigration, is the fact that we must necessarily be exercised about the question where the labourer is going to locate and what vocation he is going to be engaged in. Heretofore not very much attention has been paid to that aspect of immigration ; rather we have been bringing immigrants into Canada and letting them shift very largely for themselves. Let me deal for a moment or two with where we hope to bring our settlers from and how we propose to settle them. We propose to bring settlers in as large a way as possible from Great Britain, and to encourage as many as will come from there to settle in Canada.

speechtext:
Yes; I will deal with that when the estimates are being considered in detail. Now, we hope to encourage all settlers who will come to Canada from Great Britain, Scandinavia, Holland, Belgium, Trance and Finland. This fact must be borne in mind, however, that from a rather close investigation of the areas from which we hope to draw our settlers, there do not appear to be a very large number of people who are in a position to purchase land and establish themselves upon their arrival in Canada. So that the bulk of our immigration, or at least a large proportion of it, will naturally be of the class who will be seeking employment. And that is not confined to Great Britain alone; that condition seems to be prevalent in every country in which we have made investigations and from which we hope to encourage settlers to come here. War conditions appear to have left the people of the Old Land, one would perhaps not say in an impoverished state, but at least in such circumstances that they have not a great deal of capital that is not invested and which they can withdraw from the businesses in which it is tied up. I should say that somewhere between twenty-five and thirty-five per cent of the total number of immigrants we expect will be able to establish themselves and that means one thing: we must take steps to assist these people in the work of colonization. With that end in view I have sought the co-operation of the provincial governments throughout Canada. In some respects I take the province of Ontario as an illustration. The authorities there are engaged in immigration work of their own. They are proceeding much the same as the federal government hope to, and prefer to
carry on their own work in their London office. It is an altogether different problem with the province of Quebec. The government of that province are anxious to repatriate a large number of their citizens who have gone into the New England states. One of the striking features in connection with the migration from Quebec and the Maritime provinces to the United States, most of which comes from the rural parts, is that those people do not engage in agriculture across the line but find employment mainly in the textile industries of the New England states. The purpose of our propaganda is to induce these people to return to Canada, and with that in view we have employed Mr. Arthur Lemont to take charge of this important work.

Has the minister approximate figures showing the exodus of our people to the United States within the last year? And is that exodus ceasing, or to what extent is it still draining this country of its best type of citizens?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. In looking over the figures for some years past one is a little surprised to find that on the whole there is little variation; the number may be a little higher one year, a little lower the next year, and vice versa. I have the figures for the past few months. One of the difficulties in dealing with the figures of migration to the United States is that, if, six months after their entry, our people have not returned to Canada, they are then regarded as permanent residents of the United States and are so entered in their returns. Consequently there is a vast difference between the number of Canadians migrating to the United States and the actual number who become permanent residents. I shall go into that more fully when dealing with the United States situation.
What inducement is being offered to Canadian citizens in the United States to return to Canada?

speechtext:
For the benefit of my hon. friend I will deal with New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in a moment or two; for the present I should like to finish with Quebec. Immigration to Quebec is not being confined simply to Canadians living in the New England states. There are enterprises in the northern portions of Quebec that will require the influx of a considerable amount of labour, and I doubt if such labour will be found in Canada. I am free to say that, we are looking for it in the Old Land and want as much of it as we can absorb. This also applies to the northern portions of Ontario. We are carrying on propaganda in an endeavour to secure settlers of the type and character that will assimilate with our people, and are providing places for them to settle, on. That is what we are endeavouring to do in this scheme. I have not any brand new striking policy to offer because between two extremes I have decided to adopt the middle course, and in pursuing that course I am trying to get value for the money we expend on bringing people to Canada by keeping them here when we' get them. I take ;t that no hon. gentleman will quarrel with the attitude of my department in that regard.
With respect to the Maritime provinces, their governments were invited to send delegates to discuss this matter with us. To-day we have in England a representative who has intimate knowledge of local conditions in New Brunswick and is working in the interests of that province. The same thing applies to Nova Scotia.

With respect to western Canada, we have not been successful in getting such complete co-

operation of the provincial governments there as we have in the East. They took the ground-and I have no quarrel with it, because I took it myself when I was in charge of affairs in Alberta-that immigration is the problem of the federal government and that no expenditure under that head should be required on the part of provincial governments. I felt I was on fair ground in taking that stand when premier of Alberta, and I have no quarrel, I say, with my western friends in that respect. As in 1908-as, indeed, in the period prior to 1908, in fact, ever since the Canadian Pacific railway was built across the plains-the western provinces have been the great fertile fields for increased population so far as agriculture in Canada is concerned. I am not unmindful of the fact that it is possible in eastern Canada, especially in the northern portion of it, to establish a great many people on the land, but, they would have to be selected with a view to their adaptability to the conditions existing there. For the next decade at least the western provinces offer the most fertile field for immigration, and I want to deal with the question for a moment or two from that point of view.
Because of the conditions I have mentioned, the people on the land to-day are feeling the pinch rather severely, and I do not wonder that they sometimes question the wisdom of expenditure on the part of the government for [DOT] the purpose of bringing new settlers into western Canada, where so many people at present find it difficult to carry on. Well, if we are to sit down and fold our hands; if we are to stop immigration entirely; if we are to say that our present population is to carry the obligations connected with our railways- which, we all admit, are over-built-if we are to leave the vacant lands of western Canada as they are to-day, I think we shall be following an unwise policy. We must take steps to settle up those vacant areas. We must take steps to bring in sufficient labour to enable the farmer to carry on in western Canada. I believe that the productivity of the area that is already broken in western Canada could, by the application of sufficient labour, be increased by at least thirty or forty per cent. But that is not the scheme I have to present to the newcomer. It will be suggested to him that he can make a success of agriculture in the West or in other parts of Canada if he avoids some of the pitfalls that we have encountered in the past. If we are honest with ourselves we will admit that one of the most serious of those pitfalls has been our endeavour to own too much land. When we went westward, 160 acres looked like a
very large farm; we were not in western Canada very long when a half section did not seem to be too large; then we set about to acquire a section; and when we had done that we wanted more. The advice I propose to give to the new settler is this: not to acquire more land than he can cultivate-I do not suggest that he might cultivate 160 acres during his first year. It is a fact that in the West to-day good agricultural land along the lines of the Canadian National railway, untilled, can be purchased at from $15 to $25 an acre, or at an average of, say, $18 to $20 an acre. If a man buys a quarter-section his overhead will not be as heavy as it will if he goes on the principle of acquiring large areas.
Is it not true that a few years ago the prospective settler could get that land, not for $15 to $25 an acre, but free, and thus clear of any overhead at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is another serious problem that we have to face to-day, in addition to the problems connected with increased transportation costs.
What proportion of free lands suitable for settlement still remains in the three prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The most popular figure given is 20,000,000 acres lying along the Canadian National railway line. Put it at 15,000,000 acres, within 15 miles of railway facilities.	.
I mean homestead lands?

Does the minister think from his own experience that a man can make a living and raise a family on 160 acres in western Canada? That is, to have pasture land and everything else on it, in a thickly settled country where there are no vacant lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is better with 160 acres to start with; his overhead and interest charges are less. When he is capable of purchasing more he can do so. My experience in western Canada leads me to believe that this very
1 p.m. thing has perhaps contributed more than anything else to the difficulty experienced by the western farmer in time of stress, having regard to the conditions of hail, frost and so on that he has to contend with from time to time. If we are to succeed it seems to me that we must confine ourselves to. smaller areas and cultivate more, perhaps, with the help that we have. I am not suggesting that our wives and children should work in the fields or elsewhere, but the point is that we should not in years of stress accumulate
Supply-Immigration

an overhead that in years of prosperity we are not able to wipe off. I do not mean to say that that is an answer to all the difficulties. I am speaking of the man who comes to Canada as a settler, without any accumulated obligations of the past.
The question will be asked, why do you invite people to come here, in the face of what is taking place to-day? Well, I am simply tiying to discuss the conditions that have come about as a result, first, of overpurchase of land, and, second, of circumstances over which most of us have no control. But, I repeat that, to start with, 160 acres will not require the investment in implements and live stock that will be necessary if a larger area is taken up.
Surely the minister, himself a western man, understands as well an any agriculturist in this House that the equipment for 160 acres will farm 320 acres without any additional outlay.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Having had sixteen years' experience in western Canada, 1 believe that you do not need a full equipment to carry on from the start. The men who made successes in the early days did not try to purchase a full equipment of farm implements right from the beginning; there was rather more of the spirit of co-operation, one with the other. That is one of the difficulties to-day in western Canada.
That is nbt answering the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am trying to demonstrate how we can invite people to come to Canada with some show of their making a success. I am convinced that if a man purchases more land at the outset than he can work, there is danger that his overhead will swamp him. And then he has to consider the possible consequences if he purchases live stock as we were induced to purchase live stock to an unprecedented degree during the years of the war-and I take full responsibility for having advocated that programme. Nevertheless we found that in the period of drought we were not troubled again. But having in mind the experience of the past it seems to me that it is wise to ask: Is there no proposition, in western Canada or elsewhere, calculated to put people on the land with a decent chance of success that will appeal to hon. gentlemen?
Now let me come to the next question. One of the most serious difficulties we have to encounter in western Canada is that' of interest rates. We have always been penalized, to a greater or less degree, as against

the F,ast, in this respect; and one of the things that I am endeavouring to do is, if possible, to secure the purchase of land at a 6-per-cent rate. I am not unmindful of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company sold their holdings at that rate of interest, but they sold them on shorter terms of payment. What we propose offering to the settler to-day is land on a thirty-two-year annual payment scheme with interest at 6 per cent. We did not have to come to the government of Canada to secure money for this purpose; and let me say, in passing, that in western Canada we must get our money on short loans from the chartered banks of Canada at about the same rate of interest as that previaling in the East. It is not that we require unlimited credit; that is not the point, in many instances we have had too much credit, in many instances loans have been made too freely, and we are suffering in consequence to-day. What we want is credit to a reasonable point at the same rate of interest as prevails in the East. In my opinion that is absolutely necessary if we are to make a success of land settlement in western Canada.

Would the minister change the period of these loans? That seems to be a marked feature of the credit system of the West, that the banks give loans for short periods; whereas in the United States they have introduced a system of, say, two-year loans secured on the farm-on the crop and on the cattle.
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not want to be drawn into a discussion of the Bank Act or the suggested amendments to it; I desire to get away from it; I will have something to say with respect to the Bank Act when that proposed legislation is up for consideration. What I am doing now is simply depicting what I think are advantages that can be offered to the newcomer to-day that we did not enjoy. That is what I want to point out to the members of this House this afternoon.

May I suggest to the minister that another remedy would be the consideration of a reduction of the interest charges on payments by men who are unable to meet their obligation. For instance, on the sale of government lands when the interest has been raised to 7 per cent, that may very well be reduced to 6 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish to get into a discussion of the conditions that

Supply-Immigration
exist there at the moment. I am trying to depict the conditions under which, I think, a man can succeed if he gets a reasonable chance.
Now, I have said to you that you cannot expect to get people with a large amount of capital or that such people will come in any number. And I do not think we need worry about it; what we want is the establishment of the men with small capital, and that is why, let me say in this connection,. I have been attracted to the Canada Colonization scheme of land selling. They have been able to list these lands for a period of thirty-two years with 6 per cent interest. Sometimes I think we have not played quite fair with the vendor, or the owner, of unused lands in western Canada because in many of our provinces we have put a super-tax upon him in respect to the ownership of these very lands. Let me say, however, that I am not quarreling with the idea; I was a party to doing that believing it would hasten the settlement of our country. Because the one thing that we did need, in order to carrj our railway burden, was new settlement in western Canada, and that the settler be put upon these lands with a reasonable chance of achieving success. Now, I think I am safe in making this assertion: That with respect to all the lands that are there for purchase in the hands of private owners, very few of those owners will not be willing to sell those lands at a reasonable rate to a newcomer, or anyone else that will purchase them and put them under cultivation. That, briefly, is the hope that I entertain-that a man will be able to obtain land at a reasonable rate with a fair prospect of securing success. He will also have the advantage of whatever assistance will come in the shape of amendments to any loaning scheme or any scheme for the betterment of conditions throughout Canada generally. I do not think such plans should be confined to western Canada particularly, but at the moment we are dealing especially with that part of the country. In addition the new settler will get the same treatment that every other settler that is already in the country will receive in that particular respect.
I would not suggest that these men go a long distance from the railway, but that they be located as nearly as possible along the railway lines in western Canada and that they be given, as I propose to give them, the full advantage of the experience of the men who are field supervisors for the Soldier Settlement Board for at least the next two years. In dealing with this question let me say this:
I do not intend, nor propose, supervision longer than is absolutely necessary. I will deal with the matter of the Soldier Settlement Board when the estimates for that department are up. Suffice it for the moment to say that I think for this year, and next year, we will have to maintain that force of men, because I believe they have been the greatest contributing factor to the success of the scheme so far. Since dealing with the matter last year,-and I will give you the figures later on,-the proportion of success has been considerably greater. In spite of the fact that throughout Canada we have had, I fear, a mole or less unsatisfactory year in agriculture, the need for salvaging of the soldiers who were placed on the land has perhaps reached the lowest point notwithstanding the discouragements experienced. That, perhaps, is not' true of the province of Alberta where a very severe drought was experienced last-year throughout the northern portion, where so many of our soldiers were settled. But these field supervisors will be available. They are. at Calgary, travelling in that vicinity; they are at Edmonton, at Regina, at Saskatoon, and at Winnipeg. And we are advertising in the Old Country and elsewhere, through our agencies, the fact that the settler can come and get expert advice from these men with respect to where he shall locate, with respect to the value of the land, and with respect to how he shall take advantage of the conditions that he finds confronting him.
When were those advertisements first inserted?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
About the
first of December, I think, on the return of Mr. Smith from the Old Country.
After the 31st, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are a great many details to remember in connection with this subject, I cannot recall the exact date.

Will the minister tell us whether the governments of the western provinces are co-operating, or propose to co-operate, in this scheme, and were they represented at the conference to which the minister has already referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, all of them with the exception of the province of Saskatchewan, and that province was represented by Mr. Gardiner a day or two later.

May I ask the minister, before he leaves this point, whether he has any estimate as to the amount of capital
ioyu

that is necessary for a prospective settler to have in order to buy the land, and equip it with machinery and stock, in order to start in the modest way which he has outlined?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should say that he should have at least between fifteen hundred and two thousand dollars.
With that amount he would carry on?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I do not think the minister has answered my question. What I wanted to know was whether he could make a statement as to what quantity of free land-that is land available for homesteading -still existed in the northwest.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not catch the question. There are in the province of Alberta surveyed and ready for settlement about 4,000,000 acres of free land. In Saskatchewan there are about 5,000,000. All of that land would not be adaptable for homesteading, but that is the amount in those two provinces. I cannot give the figures for Manitoba.
How far from the railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should say from 18 to 30 miles.
Would that land be adapted to growing wheat profitably?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would say the bulk of this land would not be adapted to wheat growing, but rather to mixed farming.
The minister made a reference to the services of the field men of the Soldier Settlement Board. Would the services of these officials be at the disposal of the Western Colonization people?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have endeavoured to keep the services separate. The Canada Colonization people are dealing purely and simply with people who have money to purchase land. They have agents of, their own in the United States, who are canvassing for that purpose, and intend later, if the scheme is successful, to do so in the Old Land, but at the moment they are confining their activities to the United States. Our agents of the Soldier Settlement Board are simply advertising the fact that reliable trained advice can be had from the supervisors or the field men of the Soldier Settlement Board, and that advice, of course, cannot be utilized for the purpose of purchasing land.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the minister explain in greater detail this arrangement he has made about the supervisory services of the Soldier Settlement Board? First, to what extent are the services at the disposal of the WTestern Canada Colonization Company? Are they at their disposal to the same extent that they have rendered them in connection with soldier settlement? Secondly, what are the terms of the arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not understand my right hon. friend. He has asked me: Are these services at their disposal to the same extent as they were in connection with the soldier settlement?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Canada Colonization Company did not touch the soldier settlement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understood the minister to say he had made an arrangement whereby the functions of the supervisors of the Soldier Settlement Board could be utilized by the Western Canada Colonization Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If I said that I did not intend to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, by their settlers, by those who come and settle under them, and that he had authorized his agents to advertise for settlers to come in under the auspices of that company, and to have their services for certain purposes. Is that correct? If so, for what purpose? And secondly, to what extent do the company's settlers pay for these services?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are two distinct services. Probably I had better explain how they work out. I have thought that it would be impossible for the government to assume the responsibility through paid officials of the government-because the supervisors of the Soldier Settlement Board are paid officials of the government-to negotiate sales, to take a newcomer and act as the agent between the vendor and the purchaser. Under the soldier settlement scheme, of course, the purchase was made outright, the money paid in full and the land became the property of the government of Canada. Under this scheme there will be an agreement of sale, running over a period of 32 years, and in many cases the Canada Colonization Company, a companv doing business as agents between the vendor and purchaser, will be acting as agent for the vendor for a considerable number of years. That is one

Supply-Immigration
of the services they propose rendering the vendor. The absentee vendor, for example, may list his land with the understanding that the payments will be transmitted through their otlice annually for a period, at least until the time comes when it can be computed and a mortgage taken, which they have promised under their scheme, but in the meantime they act as agents, the same as other agents who act' between the vendor and the purchaser of land. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, we have felt there are two distinct services to be rendered. One is the service of listing the land through an agent for sale, for a period of 32 years, at the rate of 6 per cent, and in addition they are finding as many purchasers as possible for the land, but selling to all who may approach them for the purpose of purchasing land. That is the service they will perform. The services the soldier settlement supervisor will render will be that he, in a larger way, will be available to the settler coming from the Old Land, because a settler will come to him, He is the paid official of the government. A vast amount of information about the whole country is at their disposal in the offices, and the settler may go' there. He may also obtain advice from that supervisor as to the minimum and maximum amount he should pay for land in any given locality. But the real service in my opinion starts when the settler is placed upon the land, no matter what agency places him there. He is a newcomer and can have from these men the advice that is so important in the initial stages of the settlement of a newcomer upon the land. I anticipate that practically all the settlers coming from the Old Country will utilize the services of the Soldier Settlement Board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As I understand the
scheme, the company acts as the agent of sale and acts as a collector afterwards. The company gets a commission after that on a non-profit basis, but the purchaser, farmer, or the immigrant coming in has the privilege of going to the supervisor first for his advice as to purchase. The minister was careful to say he would give his advice in this form, "In this district I fix a minimum of so much an acre and a maximum of so much an acre." Then the second part of the advice is as to farming afterwards. With all deference, I suggest this to the minister's mind. He is just giving, his officers sufficient authority to get the government of the country into trouble, and not sufficient authority to be the least service to the purchaser. He puts a minimum and a maximum in a district. 70
Now there will be one farm worth twice as much as the adjoining one in the same district. Unless the department is prepared, as we did in the soldier settlement scheme, to exercise control over every purchase, it had better keep its hand out of the matter of valuations altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The report I got from the agents of the government, in the United States was that the return of at least 15 per cent of prospective settlers who did not settle in the West in the last ten years was due to the fact that they had received conflicting information. [DOT] Further we do not propose to restrict that information in a general way, although it is fair for my right hon. friend to take that inference I think. We intend to give that advice in a real way, particularly to Old Country settlers. If a man chooses a certain parcel of land, it may not be listed by the Canada Colonization Company; it may be listed by a private individual, and in almost nine cases out of ten, if the individual approaches him in that way, he will be asked eight per cent interest and, perhaps, a higher rate per acre than the land would be listed for with the Canada Colonization Company or some other corporation of that sort. But if you get your soldier supervisor as agent between vendor and purchaser, then in my opinion, you are going to have a great deal of trouble. If it were possible to purchase outright as has been the case in the past, there would be difficulty. The greatest service the supervisor has rendered- and I am not unmindful of that-is that his business was to purchase the land as cheaply as he possibly could, and purchasing it outright in that way, he invariaby got rock-bottom prices. But that does not prevail in this case.

Supposing a settler purchased a piece of land and it was discovered later that he had been absolutely defrauded; is there any redress for him? Soldier supervisors have a very large territory to go over. When the Union government appointed those supervisors in the first place, one of them told me that he no sooner got his appointment than men came to him and offered to bribe him to sell their lands to soldiers for double what the land was worth. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) touched the right point when he said that one farm lying alongside another will be worth twice as much. I have known them worth five times as much. Newcomers should be protected, and if a glaring fraud is perpetrated, there should be some supervisor who could annul the whole transaction, so that those men might not pick

up and go out of the country, cursing the country and bringing the whole thing into disrepute.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is just the service that I hope they will render. I am not unmindful of the fact that individuals will come in who will make mistakes in purchasing. The very thing mentioned by my hon. friend, that the supervisor may be offered a consideration for the purpose of assisting the vendor, would be bound to be prevalent, and to a much greater degree than if he were purchasing outright, spot cash, for the government, and, becoming the actual owner of the land for the purpose of selling it to another party. I do not think it wise that we should ask the supervisors to go into that particular service; but as regards advice-and I do not want to cover the ground again-supervisors have had some years of experience; they know the country; they have valued land in the vicinity; they ought to have a fair idea of the value of every quarter section within the agricultural district through which they travel. It is not unfair to expect that and that they could give a pretty fair value for any quarter section of land upon which their opinion might be asked.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I agree with that; but the matter is so important, and I am so confident of my position that I want to impress it again. If the minister gives them any authority, let it be complete. Do not let the minister's officials come in and give any advice unless full responsibility is taken and the most thorough investigation given individually to the land, not merely to the man. If the minister does not do that, he is going to land in this position, and I will give him warning in time. He will find afterwards that there will be throughout Canada settlers who will claim that being promised the supervision and assistance of the officers of the Dominion government, they came in and they were defrauded notwithstanding. They could easily be, under the loose system the minister has in mind; they will be back on this government and this country, and they will have a claim that will be very difficult to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know how far my right hon. friend would go, unless he went the length of making the supervisor the actual agent between vendor and purchaser.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I go to the length in
every case we go in the soldier settlement work. There the government is responsible absolutely for the fairness of every purchase. The government supervises each and all in

which it lends any money. Unless you are prepared to go that length in cases where you do not lend any money do not go any length at all.

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
I had not

In answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Beaubien) as to why the provinces did not assist, I may say that they are quite in sympathy with the settlement of these lands; but for the reason that they did not have the natural resources, they did not feel they were called upon to make any expenditure in this connection. What I hope will be of the greatest service to the settler through the Soldier Settlement Board is the advice that will be given to the settler during the first two or three years that he is upon the land. I have announced to the committee that the advice, so far as it will go, will be not to venture into too heavy investments in land, but that he will make his start in a modest way and, as he progresses, that he will purchase, if needs be, further lands in order that he may carry on. In connection with the American field, at a meeting of the agents held some months ago in Chicago, I found that while agricultural conditions in western Canada were in rather bad shape, the inflation during the war had stricken the American farmer to a worse degree than it had affected our own agriculturists throughout Canada, and that inflation in farm values across the border had gone to such an extent that the farmers could no longer carry on. Indeed, I was approached by very many American farmers with splendid equipment who were desirous of moving out of the central and western states and coming to western Canada, but who found themselves in such straits that they had not even the means to pay their railway transportation. That is the . difficulty one encounters everywhere. But I am hopeful despite that fact that a great many of these men will come to western Canada. With that thought in view we offered a scheme of leased lands to encourage them to move out of the United States and settle here.
