speechtext:
No, we have not got them by provinces. What I want to point out, however, is that from the United States and Great Britain we shall get about the same percentage of people who can establish themselves on the land. I do not expect that we shall have a large population for the year 1922-23, because immigration has reached one of its low points in Canadian history. I may give some of the figures with respect to immigration since 1881, when we had 47,000 coming into Canada, down to 1900 when it was 44,000. The next year it was 23,000 and in 1905 and 1906 we had 128,000 and 130,000. In 1910 we had 208,000; in 1911, 311,000; in 1912, 354,000 and 1913, 402,000. Then it began to drop until in 1916 we had 48,000; in 1917, 75,000; and in 1919, 57,000. In 1921-22, it was 89,000. I mention these figures to show the fluctuation there has been over that long period of years. What I have been trying to show this afternoon is that we shall undoubtedly get from the United States a fairly large number of desirable settlers who will go on the lands of western Canada, and we shall also get from Great Britain and the Scandinavian countries pepole who will ultimately become settlers in the West. We have established on the Continent of Europe agencies for two purposes; because from the Continent, owing to war conditions, there are areas from which perhaps we would not get people whom we could assimilate or absorb into the population just yet. Nevertheless there is a very large population on the Continent from
 t
which we can draw desirable settlers for northern and western Canada. Let me say, too, that the governments are becoming interested in this question. They have over-population in their countries. I know it may be said that that is one of the reasons why Great Britain wants to get rid of some of her people who are not of a very desirable type, but I shall deal with that feature when I come to the subject of assisted passages. I think it is safe to say that we are on sane ground when we claim the right to designate who may come into Canada and so afford reasonable protection to our citizens. At the continental ports we are not seeking to hold back desirable immigrants but rather to encourage them. From Bohemia we hope to obtain a very desirable class of settlers; also from Poland, Hungary and other continental countries. One peculiar outstanding fact I should mention in passing, namely, that from Hungary there promises to come a larger proportion of people in a position to establish themselves here than perhaps from any of the other countries from which we hope to draw a considerable number of immigrants.
Under our law no Hungarian is permitted to come into this country. He is regarded as an alien enemy.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Hungarians have been coming in for some considerable time by permission of the minister.
By permission of the minister?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The order in council has not been cancelled as against Hungary and other enemy countries.
Does that apply to Germany also?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Notwithstanding that we have been letting in a few Germans for whom application has been made by their friends. I am hopeful that in the near future the order in council against nationals from those countries may be brought to an end.
If those nationals are permitted to come in by order of the minister, why should not the order in council be cancelled forthwith?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I see no particular reason why it should not be cancelled. But I take it that no desirable individual is being handicapped as a result. Immigration seems to be rather a touchy subject in this House. I did not know there

Supply-Immigration
were so many tender spots that one might tread upon in dealing with the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is immigration from other countries a matter of pull too?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I would not say that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister, I understand, predicts increased immigration of a desirable class of farmers from the United States during this year, and I also understand that he predicts a decrease in the movement of our farmers to the United States. What, if any, new policy or change in policy is likely to produce the result he has predicted?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it is safe to say that in crises of all sorts you reach the peak sooner or later, that there comes a day for liquidation. I think that day has come. I may refer to my own locality, which I know fairly well. Perhaps 15 per cent of the people there have been forced out of business, nothing could save them, they had to go; there are 15 to 20 per cent in rather serious difficulties; a fair percentage of the balance is not by any means on Easy street, but there is no doubt that they are going to remain and continue in agriculture. I think my hon. friend will agree with me that the same condition of affairs applies in a business way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then I understand that the minister's prediction is based on the fact that the peak both ways has been reached, and is not due to any new policy or change in policy? In a word, it is merely an accident, so to speak. We on this side want to do everything we can to assist the minister in bringing about the most desirable conditions, but if his prediction is based on what is only an accident, surely it is time that some policy was evolved whereby the improvement should be the result of that policy and not a mere accident.

I think in the past too much credit has been taken by governments for policies that would change conditions. That they have some effect I will not deny, but not to the extent of completely changing conditions of depression or inflation. I am not announcing a policy for the government or for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), I am dealing with the question of immigration solely and am describing some of the chances of success which I think I have, or in regard to which I am optimistic to suggest to the agents of the government in the Old Country and elsewhere that they have, for inducing settlers
to come to Canada. Possibly the Minister of Finance will have something to say about the policy of the government.
The minister has taken us as far' as the prairies. Will he tell us if there is any prospect of co-operation with the province of British Columbia in respect to immigration?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall have a word or two to say about that if my hon. friend will permit me to get through with my remarks on the Old Land and other sources of immigration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I, too, have a few questions to ask, and if the minister would prefer to finish his address and deal with them when his estimates are up, I shall be very pleased to wait.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not object to any questions now except that they lead me away from what I am proposing to say. We have had a visit from the representative of the Swedish government which is undertaking to supervise emigration in a systematic way. He has gone as far as Winnipeg at the expense of the Canadian government. I suggested that he go as far as Vancouver in order to get a first hand idea of the opportunities awaiting settlers throughout Canada. He has come back enthusiastically in favour of recommending his government to send out settlers. Indeed, he is to bring over the first contingent of two or three hundred. The same thing applies to Holland. We were visited by the representative of that country and he went as far as Vancouver. He has gone back to recommend to his government that settlers be sent out to the number of 1500 as an experiment this year. These men have not very much cash to invest, and it is a matter of finding employment for them at the outset. But in a real way we have been trying to bring to the attention of the governments of the countries from which we hope to attract settlers the opportunities we have to offer homeseekers.
In respect to Scotland, a country that has done more for the settlement of Canada than perhaps any other country of its size in the world, we have been endeavouring to interest people in the northern part of that country to settle here. If I had time I could read to the committee letters from our agent, Mr. Murphy, who has gone through the northern portions of Scotland, where he says there are hundreds of men anxious to come to Canada.

What was Murphy doing in Scotland?
Supply-Immigration

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, he appears to be getting along very well with our Scottish friends there. At least, he is having splendid success in interesting those people in Canada. We hope to induce a large number of people to come from Scotland, who will be fully as able to establish themselves as those who come from England. We have not been so successful as far as Scandinavia is concerned; only in Denmark have we had an agent up to the present. In Sweden the possibilities of the settlement of their people in other countries than their own is commencing to be realized, and we hope to go into that country with our agents and propagandize for the purpose of encouraging emigration to Canada. Then, we expect to get people from Iceland and other countries where the climate is similar to that of Canada-people who will be readily assimilated here.
What about Belgium?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have an agent at Antwerp, but there is no immediate prospect of inducing many Belgian people to come to Canada. So far as British Columbia is concerned, we have had the premier of that province here. He has a very active officer in the person of Mr. Pattullo, who sent an agent to India to induce officers retired from the Indian army to come to Canada. An officer of the Soldier Settlement Board was sent there by the federal government with the same object in view. I cannot say what success they are having, but we hope that a large number will be induced to take up residence in western Canada, particularly in British Columbia, because we feel that these, people would adapt themselves more readily to the conditions in that province than in the others.

Has the government of British Columbia made a definite offer to join with the federal government in an aggressive policy of immigration in conjunction with the British government under the Empire settlement scheme? Has not British Columbia also concluded or partly concluded arrangements with the British government contingent upon the consent of the Dominion government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know that negotiations were being carried on, but I cannot say whether or not they have reached a conclusion. Ontario has carried its negotiation to a conclusion respecting immigration into that province from the Old Land. I know Mr. Pattullo was carrying on negotiations of the same sort.

Mr. LADNER. The point of my question is that the British government and the provincial governments are apparently agreed upon some sort of action. Is the Dominion government willing to co-operate in that scheme or does its policy exclude the possibility of such co-operation?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, the
British government will deal with private corporations, with municipalities, with provincial governments, or with federal governments. Indeed, in the case of Australia there are dealings with the states as well as with the Commonwealth government. Such arrangements are, of course, always subject to the approval of the federal authorities.

I wonder if the minister can say now whether or not the figures I gave the other day were correct. I pointed out that under that scheme, Canada, having taken no interest in it, got 5 p.m. only 130 immigrants as against upwards of 11,000 in the case of Australia and New Zealand. I think the minister said he was going to send the deputy minister to find out something about it; perhaps he knows now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As I recall it, what my hon. friend asked the other day was whether or not we were too late in making application for the joint action. I had no recollection of any figures being mentioned, because we have no intention of entering into a similar agreement to that made between the British government and the government of Australia, namely, for the settlement of land as well as for assisted passages. Ours extended only to the point of assisted passages.
Was the deputy sent over?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
When?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He should be in England now.

Is there a definite arrangement between the government of British Columbia and this government respecting immigration, and if so would the minister be good enough to give us some intimation of what it involves?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is
no definite arrangement between the two governments at the moment.

Supply-Immigration

But is there any working
arrangement under which immigration will be going to British Columbia just as it will be going to the prairie provinces? The reason I ask this is that according to the press the Attorney General of British Columbia has intimated that there will be a considerable demand for labour in that province this year. He says:
While not anticipating such a labour shortage as that-
Referring to a statement made by a large employer of labour.
-there is every indication that the demand for labour will be at least equal to if not considerably more than the available supply, and that there will be no justification for any man being idle.
The article goes on to show considerable activity in British Columbia. I understand the provincial government is desirous of having an early immigration policy there, not only for agricultural settlers but also for men engaged in such other business as mining, lumbering and fishing. The matter is of considerable interest to British Columbia, therefore, and we would like to have some information from the minister on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
So far as
that demand is concerned, we have no recent communication. As in the case of Ontario, British Columbia maintained an office in the Old Country and carried on a considerable amount of propaganda work on their own part, and they may be carrying it on now without my knowledge. We have been co-operating very fully with British Columbia, and we are prepared to carry on in the same way. I speak only of the demands for labour from the areas from which we have received them; I have no knowledge of any communication from British Columbia stating that they required labour of. that character.

I do not wish to be too
persistent, but will the minister be good enough to disclose the nature of the co-operation? Mr. Pattullo, Minister of Lands for that province, in an address delivered to the Board of Trade before I left Vancouver, intimated that he then had negotiations under way with the Dominion government under which a definite scheme twould be worked out to bring immigrants to the province, and that the Dominion would be a party to that scheme. If such a scheme has been arranged for, it is of importance to the province to know what it is, just as the minister has outlined a scheme of co-operation-or non-cooperation, as it appears-with the prairie provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, everything I have said with respect to the prairie provinces would apply to British Columbia, with the exception that British Columbia, through Mr. Pattullo, is taking a very much more active interest in immigration than the governments of the prairie provinces. The reason is a good one: British Columbia owns its natural resources and is setting aside land for the purposes of settlement, particularly along the Grand Trunk Pacific. I know that they are extremely anxious to promote settlement and have asked us to co-operate in bringing these localities to the attention of prospective settlers, they on their part agreeing to take care of them upon arrival. Beyond that we have no definite scheme of co-operation, except in a general way; we shall, of course, give to British Columbia or any of the other provinces any support or assistance that we can.

What is that support or
assistance? That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In bringing to the attention of prospective settlers the advantages of British Columbia, in the circulation of any advertising matter that they may provide, and so on-in a general way; because we cannot pick any particular province in that respect. Our business is to try to induce people to come to Canada, and to that end, in a fair way, to present the advantages of all the provinces to prospective settlers.

So far as that point is
concerned, is it not a fact that the Department of Immigration-under this government as under other governments-generally recommends the prairie provinces to settlers? I ask that because it is my understanding that they do. Like British Columbia, of which my hon. friend speaks, northern Ontario, from which I come, is a very fine farming section, although it has bush lands just as British Columbia has. Yet it has always been my impression that the Department of Immigration recommends the prairie provinces to the detriment of the other sections referred to. I should like a little enlightenment on that point from the minister if he can give it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's objection, if he puts it that way, is well taken; I think there is no doubt about it. In former days the lands were free on the prairies, but they were not free elsewhere. There was a charge made, if I remember correctly for lands in the province of Ontario as well as in British Columbia-not very much it is true, nevertheless a small charge
Supply-Immigration

was made for land. These provinces owned their natural resources. They were exploiting them and trying to settle the lands in their own interest, whereas in other cases the lands belonged to the federal government and that government was trying to settle them primarily in the interest of the Dominion.

Does the minister's scheme involve granting financial assistance to the settlers? Take a concrete case. Supposing John Smith from England wanted to come out here and select a piece of property in Alberta. Does the minister's scheme involve a measure of financial assistance repayable over a period of years, and does that rest upon the province, carrying the same illustration to the province of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, I would not like to be drawn into a discussion of what Mr. Pattullo has in mind for British Columbia. So far as regards the federal government, I would say "no" to eveiy one of his queries. We have not a scheme of placing people on the land and assisting them with money. I will deal with the subject of assisted passages later on.

In reference to the minister's last remark, is it not a fact that the control of immigration belongs to the federal government and not to the provinces? Consequently, the fact that a province might control its own lands should not debar that province from the benefit of the operations of the federal authorities in regard to immigration. Just along that line, may I ask-because I notice that the minister has dealt very fully with the Maritime provinces, the province of Quebec, the prairie provinces and British Columbia-did I understand him aright, at the outset of his remarks, to state that in so far as the province of Ontario is concerned they were going to do nothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh no,
what I said at the outset was that the government of the province of Ontario were carrying on a propaganda in the Old Land on their own account; they were bringing in, for example, domestic servants, they were making advances for them, they were trying to induce settlers to eome to that province; but I hope, that I did not in any way mislead my hon. friend into thinking that the federal government had no responsibility. I say we are doing just the same for Ontario that we are doing for every other province; trying to induce people to come in. We are willing to distribute literature for Ontario and willing to hold up the advantages of that province as

well as those of the other provinces of Canada. My hon. friend is perfectly right; the responsibilty for inducing people to come to the country primarily devolves upon the federal authorities. In the past, the responsibilty of the colonization end of it has rested very frequently upon anybody, but primarily upon the provinces themselves.

They were forced
to assume the responsibility. The minister has stated in his remarks this afternoon that the prairie provinces offered the most fertile field for immigration. He paid but scant attention to the requirements of the rural districts of old Ontario where I will venture to state-in view of the doleful tale we have heard from the representatives of western Canada-there is no field so fertile to-day, and no demand so pressing.

Is it not true, in spite of the emphasis laid on the three prairie provinces and the fact that the Dominion government owns the land, that if we look over the statistics for the last twenty years we find that more people have settled in Ontario than in the other provinces referred to?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend let me say that I have brought to the attention of intending settlers the portions of northern Ontario that are being opened up to-day. I cannot say how much of this has been done in the past, my hon. friend, perhaps, will know better than I. However, it is our intention to have a policy of propaganda that will bring to the attention of the settler the chances that are available throughout the whole of Canada. That is one of the things I think it is the duty of the department to do, not to concentrate absolutely on one particular part of Canada, because thei'e are advantages in every province. There are advantages, perhaps, in one province that will appeal to the individual, and that will hold him in Canada, that he will not find in the other provinces. We cannot say that any particular province is better than the other, but we can say that there are advantages to be obtained in all of them.
I do not know that I should detain the House any longer with the matter of immigration or where it shall come from. But let me emphasize this one thing before I have done: On several occasions, in speaking upon this question, I have emphasized the necessity of reasonable and careful selection; and I hope that in dealing with the matter of assisted passages it will not be inferred, as it has been said to me on some other occasions, that when we embark in an undertaking of this kind we will nc.t, perhaps, get as desir-

Supply-Immigration
able a class of settler. I do not think it should be inferred from the mere fact that some people make application for assistance to come to the country that they are not desirable settlers. I think that the evidence we have in the Old Land fully goes to prove that very many desirable people are anxious to move from their present homes, anxious to come to some new country in the British Empire to make a fresh start, but perhaps, have not sufficient means to enable them to do so. However, to that particular class our scheme does not apply. It rather is more restricted in character than that. Here let me say that one of the greatest schemes in connection with immigration that has appealed to me most is that of child emigration to Canada. In my younger days I knew somewhat of the success of the Bamardo scheme. I know that in some respects this work has been criticized, but there are organizations in the Old Land who have been doing a splendid work in this respect and the record of the Barnardo Boys Home, having regard to enlistment during the war and the success of the boys who did enlist, is a splendid record and one that will bear comparison with the record of any of the young men who enlisted in the Canadian army. From Ontario and eastern Canada-but it will apply, perhaps, to my hon. friend's province more than to any of the others and it has been the case for several years so far as I can discover from the records of the department-applications have come in excess of those that the various organizations engaged in this work are able to fill. For example, a year ago there were about 15,000 applications for boys and girls from people who were willing to take them into their homes and adopt them, and about 1,500 were placed. That gives you an idea of how close we are to the point at which we aim in connection with this work.
Now let me, for a moment, deal with the matter from a close personal standpoint. In the province of Alberta we have had for a number of years what is known as the Delinquent Children's department. That is a very poor name for it. It should never have been called by that name. It was rather a department organized for the purpose of caring for children who were unfortunate, through no fault of theirs, and very frequently through no fault of the parents, and we find, strange to say, that in the new provinces in the West, which are said to be settled by bachelors, there are always more applications for children than we are able to satisfy. Indeed, the only children in the hands of the government to-day, or a year ago, so far as I know, were those who were slightly mentally
deficient. The robust, physically fit child was adopted into a foster home as soon as he was able to go there. There is in Ontario and eastern Canada a great field for this work, and there are in the Old Country children of deceased soldiers by the thousands, children of respectable parents by the thousands, who will make splendid settlers and citizens of Canada if we can bring them here. This work has been very largely philanthropic, so far as I can ascertain, assisted by contributions of people interested in the work. Very little assistance has been given to the organizations by the government of the Old Country or the government of any country, and the recent increase in transportation rates has made it difficult for these organizations to carry on. I therefore propose to offer a grant for those who can be carefuly selected and absorbed in decent homes in Ontario, and in this work we are enjoying the full co-operation of the officials of the Ontario government who have been dealing with this phase of the question in placing these children in foster homes. The government is asking parliament to give us a reasonable sum for this work, up to $200,000, which we hope will be supplemented by the British government through their Overseas Settlement Board. I want to emphasize first the selection of the child; secondly, the selection of the home and the desirability of getting these young people into our Canadian homes. Strange to say there has been throughout Canada for the past few years a very serious lack of domestic help in the household. The Ontario government and the Saskatchewan government have been doing something during the past two or three years in connection with bringing out those girls for domestic service. Again we find the same difficulty in regard to assistance. So far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned they have been collecting from various individuals and have been putting up some money themselves, sending over and bringing girls out. I made careful inquiry of Mr. Gardiner when he was here discussing the question of immigration as to the success of their scheme, and I was assured that they were meeting with splendid success and that there was very little loss in connection with the proposition. Miss Biden, an official of our department, paid partly by the Department of Immigration and partly by the Saskatchewan government, has been an inspectional officer and has made the selections. We propose to carry out this work to a greater degree, trying to supplement the demand for domestic servants by asking for a vote of $200,000 for this purpose, which will be further supplemented by the Overseas Settlement Board.
Supply-Immigration
Is that an additional $200,000 to be asked for in the case of children?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. That however is a grant that will not be returned. In the case of domestic servants we hope that 90 per cent of the money will be returned to the federal government. So far as the child is concerned, it is absolutely a grant* in toto for the passage.
Would the minister not consider the advancement of assistance to that extent to competent farm labourers who are vouched for by the provincial authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Referring to the farm labourer, we have not ventured into that field. Perhaps my hon. friend will agree with me that I am somewhat of a careful individual with respect to the expenditure of public money. At least I know that this vote will not meet the ideals of a great many of my hon. friends in this House. They will say I should have gone a great deal further. So far as I am concerned, 1 propose to go slowly. I hope we shall get settlement. I feel that we shall get settlement and the evidence of that is that the steamship companies are having splendid success in their booking so far with people who will come as labourers to Canada.
Dealing with the other class to whom my hon. friend referred, we have no scheme for the bringing out of farm labourers. It is rather a difficult proposition to deal with, owing to .the fact that you have no assurance, or perhaps not as much assurance of holding the farm labourer or the mill labourer as is desirable, in order to secure the return of the money. But what we are doing is this: in regard to the individual who has come to Canada and has not been able so far to obtain the necessary funds to bring his family or his children, or the individual who is desirous of bringing a friend whom he knows, either from an urban centre or from a rural district and who will settle upon the land, we have set aside $200,000 for assistance, as an experiment. We provide that he shall pay 25 per cent of the cost of the passage of his family, or the family whom he may nominate, and give a guarantee for the return of the money. In order that it may work smoothly and easily, we are dealing with the local banks in this respect, taking security from two of his neighbours, because my experience since coming here is that on hundreds of different occasions we have been appealed to by men already in the

country for assistance in order to bring out their families and establish them here. We thought it would be proper to provide for the furnishing of 25 per cent, either by the individual who nominated the family, or by someone else. We provide for the return of the money in a certain period. If it is the wife alone, or if it is a family consisting of the husband and wife, a repayment inside of one year of the full amount, or if there are children within two years, without interest, according to the size of the family is required.
Is this in addition to the $400,000 already referred to?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, making $600,000 in all.

Is there a class of assisted immigrants other than those to which the minister has referred? A little while ago he referred to assisted immigrants. Does the class he has referred to include all of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it is simply assisted passages from the Old Land, with respect to which we have the co-operation of the Overseas Settlement Board. There is no programme of assisted passages from any country except Great Britain.
Does the Old Land mean Great Britain and Ireland, or what does it mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It covers the area to which assistance is given by the Overseas Settlement Board of the British government. That applies to Great Britain.

In regard to the people who are being brought out from various parts of Europe, is the government guarding against these various people settling in colonies to the detriment of western Canada, as has happened in the past? Is an effort being made to assimilate them with the people of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I might say personally that I do not favour colony settlement as we understand it in western Canada. It is a deterrent to assimilation; but we must bear in mind that on the part of many people there will be a desire to settle in communities, and indeed, this desire comes from the Old Land. One of the great attractions of the Australian scheme is that they are going to settle in communities where convenient for them. Our experience in western Canada has been that people assimilate much more readily if there is a reasonable amount of distribution of those people, rather than if

S upply-Immigration
there are close colonies of people of one nationality.
I think I have covered the ground fairly well. I anticipate I shall have innumerable questions with respect to this matter, but what I have in mind is a careful selection of the people who shall come to Canada a follow-up policy that will assist the settler, not in the expenditure of money particularly, but by advice that, we think, will be valuable to him. Not only that, but we propose to bring, as fast as labour conditions will warrant, labour into Canada. We have to-day, in both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railway offices advertisements asking the farmers to make application for the men that they can employ annually very largely upon their farms. Those men will be carefully selected and brought out to fill the requirements. In fact, we have not missed any agencies, because I take it that we are to have first carefully selected settlers, and second, when we get them into the country, some organization that can perform a service to a certain point; but above and beyond all, we must have the hearty co-operation of all the people and all organizations,>
churches and otherwise, in connection with this problem

Would the
minister go on and finish the relation of his scheme of land leasing? He touched on that, but I do not think he finished it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not intend to deal with it at any particular length, except that I would say this, that strange to say, in spite of the fact that the information we got was that a great deal of land that had been cultivated was being abandoned and that it was going back into the hands of owners, non-resident or otherwise who would not cultivate it, in Manitoba alone, the only province in which we were able to secure any considerable number of farms for the purpose of leasing, after correspondence with secretary-treasurers of municipalities, the men who ought to know best, and after a careful canvass of the whole province, all that we were able to get was 75 farms. Some of those were not, on inspection, found to be in condition to offer to any tenant, without at least one year's summer fallow. That is not a desirable proposition to offer to a newcomer to the country unless you are prepared to pay him for that operation. Our investigation in that respect did not go very far. In spite of the fact that we are told so frequently that so many of those farms will be settled but will not be occupied and worked next year, I think that is a hopeful sign and evidence in itself that things are not just as bad
as we sometimes think they are. I am optimistic enough to think that we have at least reached the peak of the depression, and that our farmers from now on will make progress, although I am not suggesting, of course, that they are going-to be inordinately prosperous.
The removal of the British embargo has had this effect. Hon. members from western Canada know what difficulty was experienced in disposing of live stock at 2 1-2 cents per pound. True, perhaps, a good deal of it, was not in a condition to market, but drought conditions sometimes forced the farmer to sell whether he was desirous of doing so or not. To-day, I am informed by Mr. Pat Burns, who is a reliable authority, that they are prepared to pay for stall-fed cattle, even as far as Innisfail, in Alberta, 7| cents per pound. This argues, in my opinion, that we can depend upon that price for export to the Old Country, and paying transportation charges from Calgary to Liverpool or Glasgow or whatever other ports these cattle are required at. This means a considerable change from the condition that formerly prevailed with respect to our live stock.
I agree with what many of my hon. friends have said in the past, that some change will have to take place in connection with the price of wheat; but there can be no serious complaint as regards dairy products. Wheat alone probably does not show any sign of advance, and any prosperity will have to come rather by way of reduction in the price of commodities the farmer must buy, and by way of reduction of freight rates upon the commodities upon which we have to pay transportation charges.
I have tried in a general way to cover this question. In some respects, it has been a great pleasure to study and discuss this question. There are as many different ideas as to what should be done with respect to immigration, I sometimes think, as there are people in Canada, and my view is, just as I said at the outset, that we must not adopt the extreme opinion of either party, on the one hand that there is no solution; that we should stop this thing outright; or on the other, that we should embark upon a programme of large expenditure of public money to purchase privately-owned land upon which to place settlers and perhaps, have a very undesirable result when such a scheme is worked out. My recommendation is that we should adopt a middle course. That is the recommendation I have made to the government of the day, and my recommendations have been accepted by the government. I hope they will bring about the desired re-
Supply-Immigration

suits. I do not believe that it would be desirable to have a huge influx of immigrants; but I hope this scheme will bring about an increase this year over last year and that, in the end, we shall get back to the state of affairs of 1913 and 1914, because we can, under reasonable conditions, absorb iij Canada quite acceptably three or four hundred thousand people a year.
Let me say in conclusion, that it is my desire, so long as I have charge of this department, to administer it so that the benefits of immigration and incoming settlers will be available to all the provinces of Canada. I dwelt upon the western provinces merely because our railway mileage there has in its vicinity a large acreage of desirable untilled land that, I believe for the time being, offers, perhaps, the best opportunity or one of the best opportunities to be had throughout Canada.

I think the minister led the committee to expect from him a statement with regard to the personnel and status of the Canada Colonization Land Corporation, as this company is apparently to act as a medium between the speculator or land holder and the settler.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Canada Colonization Company, as I understand the matter, has had rather a stormy career in endeavouring to carry out a land settlement scheme that was projected by Mr. M. A. Brown, of Medicine Hat, who went throughout Canada and induced a large number of men of influence and financial means to back him in this scheme of settling, in the first instance, the privately-owned lands of western Canada. I well remember when they came to interview the government of the province of Alberta, they were accompanied by General McRae, who was then manager of the company. They had a scheme for the compulsory listing of lands for a period of two years! This would require legislation by the provincial governments and was rejected; and upon that scheme they spent about a year. I know it is a most difficult thing for an organization of this kind to obtain a satisfactory arrangement under which to carry on its work. But we do need some sort of organization such as this to take the place of the individual who has made a business of land selling for profit. That such a need exists there is not the slightest doubt in my mind, particularly as conditions exist to-day. We have not free lands to offer people within reasonable distance of the railways; all the lands that are desirable are held by private owners. It is
[Mr. C. A. StewartJ
difficult when you reject a scheme of purchasing .these lands outright and re-selling them to find some other plan which the government can embark upon with any protection to its officials, as outlined by the leader of the Opposition this afternoon. I quite realize that, and I have repeatedly gone over the matter trying to devise a scheme that would keep the government out of difficulty. Now, this organization adopted a scheme of charging a certain percentage of the sales for the service they rendered the private individual.
What is the percentage?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Ten per
cent. I cannot see any objection to a scheme of that kind. These men do not propose to make any profit out of this undertaking; nor do I see how they could make a profit. On the basis of paying to the agent what he legitimately gets for bringing people into the country it will cost them at least a dollar per acre. They have in the United States to-day, I am credibly informed, sixty agents who are operating on a commission basis, who receive for their service something like ten per cent per acre. Hon. gentlemen can figure that out. On a basis of $18 per acre for land, they will get $1.80 per acre for the handling of the land. On the other hand they have the responsibility of going to the vendors, getting the listings of these lands and acting as the agent of the vendor for a period of six or seven years at least,-I am now speaking of the non-resident vendor-thus rendering a service not only to the vendor but to the people of Canada; because to bring in a settler who is located properly, with a decent chance of paying his interest and of having his - payments extended when they are due, is certainly rendering a service to the people of Canada that is of some value. Now, a certain proportion of the balance of that money will go to the local individual who assists the agent in that respect. True, if they do not interest the prospective settler from the United States or elsewhere and the settler comes in and purchases without an effort on their part, that dollar will be saved. But that does not happen in a very great number of cases. I am informed that there are at the moment nearly 900,000 acres of western land listed which they can sell on the terms I have outlined, namely, over 32 years and at a rate of 6 per cent. And they propose to spend all the money that they get on that 10 per cent basis in an endeavour to bring people into the country. The arrangement

Supply-Immigration
I have made with them is that they shall settle on the land as a minimum 200 heads of families this year. That is the minimum which I think we should require. I am trying this purely and simply as an experiment, hoping to establish people permanently in that way with a decent chance of getting on.
Can they settle anywhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Allow me to finish, please. If we do not adopt some plan of that kind, what will happen? You will simply put the prospective, settler again at the mercy of the private landowner or his agent, and I need not ask any hon. gentleman from western Canada what that means. We all know that the settler will be asked 8 per cent, the prevailing rate in western Canada. And as I have experienced on many occasions, , the moment you go to purchase from the private owner, if you appear anxious to have the property he owns you invariably find the price increased .particularly if you are a newcomer. The same experience is reported by the immigration agents in the United States. They' are asking for an organization to which they can send men with the assurance that they will get a fair deal and that they will not come back dissatisfied because of conflicting reports they hear from various points they visit in western Canada. I hope that we shall save some money ultimately in connection with this attempt on our part to carry out the colonization end of the scheme in a definite way for the settlement of people in western Canada. The manager of the company is Mr. Everett. He is the man in whom I stake my confidence for the success of the scheme. As regards Mr. M. A. Brown, he was the originator of this scheme and is again about to raise money. He has met with difficulties and I am not prepared to criticize him. I know that he has been criticized very severely in many quarters, and many of the individuals who backed him at the start say he changed the programme, that another scheme was attempted, and that they were not consulted and are not prepared to put up money. On the other hand, there are still behind him a number of ardent supporters who are putting up their money in order that the scheme may continue. So much for him. But the man on whom I depend to make a success of the undertaking is Mr. Howard Everett, who has had many years experience in land settlement in western Canada. He is an American and was at one time manager of the Luse Land Company who settled a great many people throughout central Saskatchewan and central Alberta. This company did a
tremendous business in the early days, as the people of Saskatchewan may remember. This gentleman thoroughly understands the business in which he is engaged, and he thinks he can make a success of it. I hope he can. I hope he will make a huge success of it, because it means that he is bringing in and settling people on the land and giving them an opportunity which they would not otherwise get if it were not for this private corporation which is not taking profits out of the enterprise.

Before the minister entirely concludes, I want to correct something I said this afternoon in connection with the question of advertising. I said that the amount spent outside of Great Britain was $92,000; it is only $90,000. But I want to draw the minister's attention to this fact. I have Hansard before me and I find at page 540 the statement that the amount spent in advertising carried on in Great Britain was $3,089.82, and in other countries $90,595.81. The minister says this return was amended. I turn to the next day's Hansard but I find that the correction has absolutely nothing to do with that question. I have been unable to find it amended anywhere else and these figures are not correct. The minister should tell us where the correction is to be found and how it was made. The House has a right to rely upon the answers given by ministers in the ordinary way, and I want to be entirely fair to my hon. friend. The day that answer was given, and he realized the frightful discrepancy in the figures, he came over to me and said that there must be some error. If there is an error we must have it corrected quickly. I have heard nothing since from the minister. I can well imagine his astonishment at the figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend's statement is hardly in accordance with what happened. After a note reached me from my secretary saying that a mistake had been made with respect to the advertising in Great Britain, and that instead of giving the full amount it merely referred to the newspaper advertising, which was $3,000, I went over to my hon. friend and told him that I would get a correction of the statement for him the following day. The correction was prepared by Mr. Stead's department and left in the hands of my secretary. The only reason I can conceive for the delay is that he was taken ill and possibly did not forward the statement.

Mr. Chairman, evidently the secretary is sick this time. The
Supply-Immigration

hon. minister did not tell me anything about that- before. If the statement is wrong, cannot we get the facts now as to how much money was spent? How many more shuffles are we to have?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understood the figures were corrected in Hansard. I will undertake to get the figures to my hon. friend and also to place them on the Table without further delay.

Are the various provinces which are co-operating with the government ready to grant free land to settlers? Is it not-a fact that the province of Quebec has extensive areas of land upon which improvements have been made in the way of the erection of houses and barns ready for intending settlers? And is it not also a fact that the Department of Colonization, of Quebec is ready to sell these lands to settlers under very favourable conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I
think I mentioned that early in the afternoon. We are co-operating very closely with the government of Quebec through the Deputy Minister of Colonization.

Am I correct in inferring from the minister's remarks that this land corporation are to receive 10 per cent on the purchase price of the lands they dispose of and also about $ 10,000 per month from the government, and that they on their part, according to the arrangements made, are to bring out at least 200 families? In other words, are they to receive $600 per family as a bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I merely say that that is the minimum. It is hoped they will exceed that very substantially.
They get $120,000 if they bring out 200 families?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. They get $100,000. It is not $10,000 per month for twelve months, but for ten months.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Supposing the company fail to live up to the conditions laid down, what penalty is provided?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only penalty one can provide in such a case is to stop further payment. That is one of the reasons why we have a provision for payment by the month. Largely the settlement will be made before the taonth of August.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I presume there is an agreement signed between the department and the company?	.	. *

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the proposed agreement. It is not signed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would take it for granted
that there would be a written agreement for such an important matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If that is so there is not the same necessity for a penalty. But I would suggest to the minister, if it is the intention of the department to enter into an agreement with the company for a period of years, that it should contain a forfeiture clause in case the company fail to make good; in other words, the agreement should then come to an end.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Month by month they are to report to the government the actual settlement accomplished, and if there is no reasonable prospect of their reaching the minimum we are to cease to do business with them. That is the proposed agreement which is not signed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I may be wrong, Mr. Chairman, but I am of opinion that a company putting up a large sum of money to engage in this undertaking would want an agreement from the department for a certain term of years.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

Is it in contemplation to relax the general regulations regarding labour other than farm labour?

speechtext:
Wherever
there appears to be necessity for labour we are prepared to pass it into Canada.
Skilled or unskilled?

Although
there is a prospect, I am told, in the building

trades in the eastern cities particularly, of a shortage of skilled labour, it has not appeared yet.

In view of the fact that
$40,000 has already been paid to this company, according to the return laid on the Table the other day, I presume that some results have been achieved in bringing families to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know that any families have been brought forward to date. Indeed, it would be rather a mistake to do so at this season. Arrangements are being made for parties to come out. I can only speak authoritatively of two such parties, namely, a number of Polish farmers who are coming with a view to purchasing land for themselves and interested compatriots, and a number of Danish farmers. From Iowa agents are coming forward with parties as soon as weather conditions will permit of inspection of land.

The minister has stated that there is a large quantity of land fairly near the railroads owned by absentee parties. Has he considered the propriety of instituting some system of taxing that land into use so it may be rendered cheaper for those who want it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend lived out west he would realize that unimproved land is being severely taxed. The taxes in many cases are 25 per cent higher on unimproved land than on improved land. So the absentee owner is being taxed.
Is there a prospect then of the land returning to the Dominion shortly so that free grants may be made to settlers?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
answer that.

Presuming that the returns brought down are correct with regard to the $3,000 spent on newspaper advertising in Great Britain, does it not seem a very large amount of money for the desperate efforts that are being made to get British settlers over here at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is very little reduction in the number of people coming from the Old Land over last year or the preceding year. Taking the figures as a whole, they would not indicate any very serious falling off. Indeed, the' serious falling off is from the United States; in that case the figures dropped to about 19,000 last year.
Is my hon. friend quite right there? My recollection is to the contrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If I have quoted the figures wrongly, I shall be glad to be corrected.

Perhaps the minister will give us the figures now. My recollection is-and I think we had it up before- that the year before last, British immigration and foreign immigration were in the ratio of 5 to 1, and that last year that dropped down to something less than 2 to 1.

I have the figures under my hand. They are divided into English, Irish, Scotch and Welsh, but the totals show that in 1920 there were about 60,000, in 1921 about the same number, and in 1922 abont 34,000; so that they were practically cut in two.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What period in 1922 does that cover?
The figures are furnished by the Bureau of Statistics. The years are given, 1913, 1914 and so on up to 1922, without any indication of what period is covered.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then the figure for 1922 would cover the nine months to December 31.

I think it is about time 1 made a little explanation.' I hold in my hand a memorandum from the Western Canada Colonization Association on which my name appears as one of its directors. I am fairly familiar with all' the circumstances connected with the organization of that association. Two or three years ago-I am not sure of the date-when the organization was first formed I took an active part in it. I attended three or four meetings, but I never received any remuneration for my services, and I never asked for any, so that I have no pecuniary interest of any kind in the organization. I am familiar with the scheme that the association outlined, and with its operations. The only criticism I have to offer would be that the percentage going back to meet the cost of operation of the scheme might be considered a little too large. The weakness I saw in it from the beginning was this: I did not think much privately-owned land would be bought by the association. The average private owner of land does not care very much to sell it on the basis of repayment in thirty-two annual instalments.

speechtext: The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.

When the House took recess I was making some little explanation in connection with my relations with the Western Canada Colonization Association. I do not suppose the House is very much interested in the matter. However, when I noticed my name on the letter head of the association I thought, perhaps, some other member might have a sheet of the same kind and make an allusion to it in the expectation that they were throwing a bombshell by announcing that I was one of the directors of that association. That is my reason for making this explanation. I may say however that I have no apologies to offer for any connection I have had with this association. Looking into the scheme which it is promoting I believe it has some merit and deserves a fair trial. It is better, perhaps, than the old system of the land colonization companies that got large tracts of land and sold them at the highest price they could possibly get. In this case we know the percentage of profit that is going to the colonization association. I understand that the association has been promised approximately $1,200,000 of subscriptions towards its scheme, and I think that about $150,000 has already been paid in in cash-that is outside of any assistance they have received from the government. I never had time to attend any of their meetings, except one or two when the association was first formed. The only objection that I had to the scheme at that time was, that there were several officers connected with the association that were drawing larger salaries than, I think, their services entitled them to. However, since that time those gentlemen have severed their connection with the association.
In the province of Manitoba I have a comparatively busy time, being associated in a semi-public way with quite a number of organizations, and I never found time to attend any of the meetings of this association. Consequently I made up my mind that when I was not familiar with the inner workings of the. association I did not want to share any responsibility. During last session, after being elected a member of the House,
[Mr. Forked
I sent in my resignation to the secretary of the association and understood it had been accepted. In looking at the paper I have before me I notice the letters "M.P." are omitted from my name so I suppose that, the letter head on it is the old one. I am not making this explanation as an apology. I have nothing against the association. I believe its work merits a fair trial. Upon the face of it the scheme has merit. But I would like to say this: If any member of the House, if any of the hon. members behind me, have any criticisms to make let them do so because if there is anything wrong with this scheme we want to know it. Let the criticism offered, if any is made, be fair criticism, and when the item comes to be voted we will know exactly what to do.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I look upon the subject before the committee, that of immigration, as one of the most important of the session. To a large extent my sympathies were with the minister this afternoon. I am not here to criticize, I am rather here to assist, and I hope that that will be the attitude of hon. members, in this part of the chamber anyway. If they have any criticism to offer by all means let us have it if it is helpful and calculated to assist in the solution of this problem. That kind of criticism, I think, is what we will get. The minister has a difficult problem to solve and he is perfectly aware of the situation. He knows all the circumstances that attend immigration, the difficulties of getting the immigrant and properly settling him on the land once we induce him to come to the country.
I heard a good deal this afternoon about the claims of the different provinces in connection with this matter. That brings to my mind just how many difficulties surround the carrying on of the government of this Dominion. Each province sets up its claim for some attention. It is perfectly proper that it should do so; but I think the explanation why the prairie provinces got more attention in the years gone by with respect to immigration is perfectly evident if we once look at the matter impartially. We had out west great stretches of free land, the best agricultural land, perhaps, that you could find anywhere, land easily broken up. This offered great attractions to incoming settlers, the consequent influx of settlement helping to pay the obligations of Canada and also furnishing a large market for eastern manufactures; and although available lands in other provinces merited attention it was quite natural, altogether apart from the fact of the Dominion government owning the land in the West, that special attention should be paid to peopling the lands that

Supply-Immigration
were so eminently fitted for early occupation.
I would like to say a word here in connection with the land in the northern part of the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba, and perhaps in Saskatchewan also. A large amount of that land is bush land, requiring a great deal of work to clear. I do not know how hon. members may feel on the subject, but I think that to settle that land would require a different type of settler; we require a man who will go in there and live what you may call the simple life. I may be wrong in my belief, but I think the only way to get those lands settled will be by inducing people to go in there and clear an acre or two, raise some vegetables and grain, keep a few cattle, and perhaps, work out in the summer and resort to lumbering in the winter. I may be wrong because I am not very well acquainted with northern Ontario. I do know, however, the character of the land in northern Manitoba; and I am perfectly sure that to get the right class of settlers you will have to go to Europe and induce some of those people who are hardy and eminently fitted for clearing up land of this description to go in there and settle. In the case of the lands that we are dealing more immediately with at the present time, it is, perhaps, a different problem altogether.
I now want to say a few words about the condition of agriculture. I would not have mentioned agriculture at all in this debate had the Minister of the Interior not made frequent reference to it this afternoon. The intimation has been made that perhaps the members in this part of the chamber dwell a little too much upon the ills of agriculture at the present time. I am convinced, however, that a little examination of the subject would ' enable hon. members to see that the condition of agriculture is a very vital question, and one that affects the welfare of the whole Dominion. No matter what our interests may be, we must feed ourselves, and we must withal have something with which to clothe ourselves. Agriculture is the greatest of all industries and one of the most essential to humanity, and even to-day, in this wonderful country of ours, we recognize the fact that if agriculture is not prosperous all suffer alike. I mention that because I want hon. members to realize that while we dwell upon the drawbacks or ills from which agriculture suffers at the present time, we are quite aware that other [DOT] industries are suffering and other people have difficulties that seem perhaps as large to them as the difficulties of the agriculturist seem to him. We realize however that agriculture is a basic industry and must be made profit-71
able, and when it is prosperous other industries begin to prosper.	.
Then, the question immediately arises: Why are you asking immigrants to come here when you find agriculture in the condition in which it stands to-day? We can answer this question. I hear from the Old Land sometimes that agriculture is in a deplorable condition over there, and I do not think we need be at all afraid to ask the people to come from the British Isles and throw in their lot with us in Canada. I think the very best brains of the country are needed to solve the problems of agriculture. It seems to me we are in a very difficult position. I quoted the words of Lord Shaw, who was a visitor here, when he referred to the conditions in Canada, and said that it was a crime that 9,000,000 people should be in possession of half the continent and unable to develop the resources. It is no use talking all the time about the great latent wealth of our country in natural resources.
It is about time we quit talking in this strain and started to do something to develop those resources. We have latent wealth, but a section of land uncultivated is no use to us except to grow grass and prairie flowers, and the mines and minerals under the soil are no use unless they are mined. Consequently, if we are going to get the benefit of the natural wealth of our country we must have men and money. These are two essentials to the development of the country. We know our economic conditions. We have a great land. We have provided facilities for a very much larger population than we have to-day, and if we had that larger population the overhead expenses-that is the expenses for the government of the country, the railways and other matters-would not be increased, but the number of people who bore ' these expenses would be greatly increased, and the burden would be made much lighter for all.
As I said before, agriculture is depressed everywhere, and the conditions here are no worse than they are anywhere, perhaps, in the world to-day as regards that industry. We hear a great deal about the prosperity of the United States. There is no doubt a great industrial boom there, but I do not think the husbandman in that country is so very prosperous at the present time, notwithstanding what we might call the industrial prosperity of the United States.
Looking back, recalling my own experience, I can realize that if the agricultural population is going to be prosperous, the agriculturists will have to help themselves to a

nos
