very large extent. We are dwelling upon our economic evils. We believe a great many
things can be improved and circumstances made better for those engaged in this calling. Nevertheless, I believe that the remedy is in the hands of the people themselves. I think hon. members will excuse me for dwelling more particularly on the prairie provinces, as that is the land with which I am best acquainted. It seems to me to-day that different methods will have to. be adopted, if the farmer is going to succeed. We will require to have small farms, more intensive cultivation, and what might be called mixed farming. The day of wheat growing has gone by, and I am perfectly satisfied that even, under present conditions, life can be made quite pleasant on a prairie farm. I know that some people will be prepared to differ with me. I know the circumstances in the West, just as well as the Minister of the Interior, knows them. The one depressing fact in the prairie provinces is that farmers are loaded down with debt. Were it not so, there would be nothing disheartening in the situation, but that is in reality the position. I believe that we can only help ourselves by having more people to develop that country and to till the prairie soil.
I wish to say a few words about the class of immigrants that we ought to get in this country. We hear a great deal about selected immigrants, I am not one of those who want what you might call indiscriminate immigration. We have a pretty mixed population even at the present time. I will read a short extract describing the sort of people we have in western Canada. We have representatives of every race, creed and tongue under the sun. This extract reads:	.
Here we have representatives of every race, creed and tongue under the sun. Chinese, Hindu, Japanese, German, Austrian, Hungarian, Russian, Italian, Pole, Swede, Scandinavian, et al. Fifty-three nationalities, speaking 89 languages and dialects and subscribing to 73 religions and creeds. One man of eveiy 12 living in Saskatchewan is a Ruthenian; one in every 5 living in British Columbia is a Chinaman; 46 per cent, of the population of Saskatchewan is non-English. Winnipeg has the second and Regina the third largest foreign-born population of any cities in the Dominion of Canada.
So that we have a pretty polyglot representation in the western provinces, and perhaps to mix them too much might be rather dangerous. But I am not afraid of the hardy peasant who is willing to go on the land. I do not care very much where he comes from. Of course, ' the better class of immigrants for Canada will be always from the British Isles and from northern Europe.
With reference to selected immigrants, I think it is nothin,- more than an intolerable [Mr. Forked
crime to bring, say the London citizen, who never saw the prairie land and knows nothing about prairie life, and place him in an Alberta shanty. We should only bring here people who are fit to live in our country and understand something about the conditions of rural life. We talk a great deal about our country. I am just as proud of Canada as any one, but we have here a very rigorous climate. We have quite a number of months of severe winter, and it must be borne in mind that the people who are to come here and go on the soil and develop the farms of the country must be of vigorous and virile character. To bring to Canada people who are unsuited is both a crime against them and a wrong done to the country to which they come.
Another matter that should be taken into consideration as regards bringing immigrants into this country is the channels through which they pass. I happened to be associated with immigration about twenty years ago, when there was a large flow of immigrants into this country, and I know something about the system that was adopted in Great Britain and in some parts of Europe in securing those immigrants. I should like to give this information to the minister. If he wants to get the right immigrants, he will have to get thg right people on the other side to select them. This work cannot be done from this side of the water; it must be done by the people who are in control of the situation over there. The Minister of the Interior of that time, then the Hon. Clifford Sifton, had a most wonderful system of organization, perhaps the best system of getting immigrants that we have ever had in this country. I know he has been blamed for letting down the bars and admitting into Canada some immigrants who should never have been here. I question very much the truth of that assertion. I think it will be found that a good many of the undesirable immigrants that came to Canada, came at a later date rather than during his regime. I will repeat that one of the methods to get proper immigrants to this country is to employ on the other side the proper agents who understand the situation, who can sift the immigrants and see that only the right kind sail for Canada. I have no doubt there are in the Department of the Interior officials who understand something about the system and who will be willing to help as much as they can in tjiis matter of selecting immigrants.
I speak with all due caution, as I do not want to say anything that will reflect upon the minister. I am going to tell the committee only what I have heard. I have heard

Supply-Immigration
sometimes that the Department of the Interior has been a dumping ground for inefficients from other departments. I am only repeating this from what I have heard.
The hon. member should not believe all he hears.
I am rather simple in some ways and, perhaps, I should not believe everything I hear.
Is it not a fact that these officials are appointed by the Civil Service Commission?	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That does not apply apparently to editors of Liberal papers.
That seems to stick in the crop of the leader of the Opposition.

I am beginning to wonder just where I come in. When I was in the Old Country and connected with the immigration service, there was in vogue a system that I did not like, namely, that of subsidizing steamship companies. I do not know whether that is done at the present time to any extent or not. We found in different towns and villages agents of steamship companies who had no regard at all for the truth. According to them, this was an Eldorado, a land of sunshine and happiness, and anyone who came to Canada was blessed. With the steamship companies, the question was one of numbers, and quality had no place in their calculations. I do not know what the system is to-day; but I would certainly be opposed to granting steamship companies a subsidy for every immigrant they brought over. I would find some other method of assisting passages.
Where should immigrants be sought? I believe to-day you can find in the British Isles many immigrants of the very best kind, young agricultural labourers, whom I could, without hesitation, advise to come to Canada, knowing conditions as I know them as they exist here to-day. We have had some pretty good immigrants come to Canada as agricultural labourers. I would refer the committee to the premier of Alberta, Premier Greenfield, the premier of British Columbia, Premier Oliver, and the premier of Saskatchewan, Premier Dunning. They all came over as immigrants, a pretty good sort, and it was a pretty good thing also for themselves that they came over.
Likewise the hon. gentleman himself.

I am very modest, as hon. members know; but I have found it a pretty good thing to come to Canada.
I should like to say just a few words as regards taking care of the immigrant after he comes here. I can well recollect the feeling that I had many years ago when I bade farewell to my native land and turned my face toward this land of hope. There is a good deal of sinking of the heart and of wondering just what the future holds for one. You come across the wide ocean amongst strangers, first impressions have a great deal to do with what you are going to think of the land to which you are coming to make your home, and I should like to see these immigrants, when they set foot upon these shores, receive a very hearty welcome. I have never forgotten the first experiences that I had at Halifax. I do not think it is at all derogatory . to me to say that I crossed the ocean forty years ago as a steerage passenger. I can well remember our being herded at Halifax just like so many sheep or cattle, and I can as. sure hon. members that the experience was not very pleasant. I have, visited Quebec and Montreal since then, and I am happy to say that conditions as they exist to-day are differ-, ent from those that prevailed forty years ago.
I would, however, repeat that there is nothing like giving immigrants a hearty welcome. I know the hearts of the Canadian people are kind anyway, and immigrants are most likely to receive a welcome.
The immigrant should be looked after upon his landing in this country in order to see that he is not taken advantage of, because there are in Canada, as elsewhere, dishonest persons who will take advantage of innocent people. I have looked into the soldier settlement scheme, and while some other speaker to-night will, perhaps, take up that subject and enlarge upon it to a greater extent than I am going to do, I believe in the soldier settlement scheme we have the nucleus of a system that might be widened out to great advantage in dealing with other settlers who ,come to make their home amongst us.
Let me say a few words as regards the drift to the south. I have under my hand some statistics, but I think most of them have been mentioned this afternoon. I do not think any government is to blame for the drift of people from Canada to the south. I do not care what government or what conditions we have in Canada, there always will be, to some extent, a drift of our people to the great republic to the south of us. It will have the attraction that numbers have; that the unknown has, and young and ambitious people, no matter what Canada may be, no doubt will, at times, drift over the line and leave us for the time being. We have, undoubtedly a rigorous
Suppl y-/ mmigra tion

climate, and older people may find it to their advantage to move to a warmer climate. I only hope older people will see their way to go over the mountains and, perhaps, find what they want in British Columbia in our own country. Almost a tragedy of the western prairies has been the fact that people have gone out to the West, have developed a farm, have made a home and become fairly comfortable, and then as old age has come on, they have'felt they would like some milder climate, so they have sold their farm for a good price and moved away instead of their wealth remaining in this country to beautify and develop the original home in which they have made their money. This is something we cannot help; it will perhaps always remain so, and it to some extent explains the drift that goes over the line to the south of us.
There is another percentage of our population that goes south that we can very well do without. Perhaps there is at the present time an abnormal' crossing of the line. I think I said before that there is what might be called an industrial boom in the United States to-day. I do not know if anyone can explain just how this boom is coming about. Agriculture is not what one might call in a first class condition there. If the wages are high on the other side of the line our artisans and labourers will inevitably drift there and you cannot keep them back. Most of the young men that go, although they are Canadians, experience no difficulty in making the change; their belongings can be packed into a club bag or satchel, and they can very easily cross the line, perhaps never to come back. These are the conditions that we must face. I know that some of my friends will not agree with me, but in my opinion, in seeking immigrants we must not draw the line at agriculture. If we can get abourers and artisans I believe we can find room for them here, because I think it will be found in the not distant future that there will be a shortage of labour of that kind in the Dominion if the United States continues to prosper industrially as it seems to be doing to-day. Well, it may be said, if such people come into Canada they too will drift across the border. However, that may be, I have no doubt the tide will turn some day, and not very far in the future either.
It must be perfectly evident from what I have said that I am much in favour of a vigorous immigration policy, although I do not know that many of my friends will agree with me in this respect. This is a matter of opinion, but I would be in favour of the appointment of a minister of immigration and 
colonization who should have charge entirely of that work. I believe the present acting minister (Mr. Stewart) is overloaded with work. While undoubtedly he is capable, I think he has more to do than he can properly attend to. I am not finding fault with him, nor criticising in any way what he has done, but I think the position is important enough and requires enough ability and energy to necessitate the appointment of a minister who shall be solely charged with the duties of this office. I am prepared to foster a vigorous immigration policy, because I do not believe that our circumstances are ever going to be improved if matters remain as they are to-day. How are we going to get along if we do not take some vigorous steps in the direction of increasing our population? We say that we have hard times and are burdened with high taxes and more railways than- we need. Well, are we going to sit idly by and see our people drift south while our own population dwindles and our burdens grow heaver? Are times going to improve under such a policy of inactivity? I believe that the times can and will be improved if we double our population. If we do that, instead of making things worse it will make them better for us; and I do not believe that the people of Canada would have anything to regret in the result. Now, I think perhaps I have spoken long enough. I am willing to assist the minister in this work, in anyway in order to see it carried forward successfully. Referring again to the colonization scheme, I have looked into proposals of the Western Canada Colonization Association and I think the scheme has merit. If there is any weakness in it, however, by all means let, us hear about it and criticise it and, if we think it is wrong, withhold the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend in all that he has said, except one statement he made, namely, that my department is the home for the derelicts of the other departments. I should like to know where the hon. gentleman got that information. I have only one officer in the department, Mr. Lynton, who was formerly in the Department of Agriculture, who has come from any other department of government to any of the four departments of which I have charge.
I am rather sorry the minister took it so seriously; I simply hear the statement and have no proof of it.

The hon. member has
mentioned several organizations that want to stop immigration. Can he tell me of any people's organization that is asking for increased immigration?

I am not speaking for any
organization, but I think I am voicing the opinion of the large majority of our people when I say that we do want immigration; and when my hon. friend's leader endorses that opinion, perhaps his remarks will have more weight with the hon. member than anything I may say. It seems to me to be deplorable that we should allow such an immense country as this to go to waste; and that anyone should ask such a question as my hon. friend puts to me is certainly unreasonable, to put it as mildly as I can. We have in northern Ontario, an area extending from North Bay on the east to the Manitoba boundary on the west, embracing from three hundred to three hundred and fifty thousand square miles, nearly as great as France and Germany added together, where they have considerably over 100,000,000 people, and yet in this area we have only 150,000 people. These figures are so simple to realize that they show to my mind the absolute necessity of bringing in more people.
Supply-Immigra tion

And may I say that I regret that this government and previous governments-for I am not criticizing the present government particularly in this matter-and the provincial government of Ontario have neglected northern Ontario? It has been neglected as have northern Quebec and northern British Columbia, because they are all bush lands. I put a question to the minister this afternoon, and he very honestly answered it as other ministers in previous governments would have done, that northern Ontario, northern British Columbia and northern Quebec did not get the advertising from the Dominion government that the prairie provinces got. I understand the reasons-that the prairie lands are held by the Dominion and are more easy to cultivate. But there are throughout the northern European countries people who prefer to go into bush lands, just as I am informed the French Canadian pioneer has the same preference. Consequently I believe it should be the effort of this government, even if it has not been of past governments, to bring into northern Ontario as many of this class of settler as possible.
I mention northern Ontario particularly, and for this reason. This country unfortunately is divided into five great sections: the Maritime provinces in the East, then Ontario and Quebec, with different ambitions and different interests; then that great section of northern Ontario; then the prairie provinces, also with different ambitions and different interests; and finally British Columbia. But northern Ontario, the section from which I come, unfortunately divides into the East and the West this great country, and until that vast area is more fully populated it will continue to form a chasm separating the East from the West, and help to keep alive, and perhaps intensify, differences which I regret to say already exist to too marked a degree in this country.
We have in northern Ontario, northern Quebec and northern British Columbia millions of acres of land and, as the minister has pointed out. in the prairies we have from 15,000,000 to 20,000,000 acres of land within reasonable distance of railways. There are in Europe tens of millions of people anxious to get out of that militaristic battleground and start life anew in this country; and I believe now is the ideal time for the government to do everything possible to populate these vast areas with the. best type of agricultural workers-and, as we know, these always form the best type of citizens.
Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but the increasing of our population with the proper fMr. Manion.]
type of immigration will help to cure the two great ills with which we are now afflicted-the railway problem and the tax problem. These two problems can be solved in only one way. We have overbuilt our railways for such a small, population by twenty or thirty years, and, of course, we spent an enormous amount of money on the war. By increasing our population we shall be creating greater traffic for our railways and lessen the burden of our national debt and taxes.
Every fair-minded man admits that conditions in western Canada have been bad during the last two or three years. I think everyone who is not blindly prejudiced will admit that the farmers of the prairie provinces have had difficult conditions to contend with in that period. But I am only speaking from the standpoint of the ordinary citizen when I say that I do not think the real reasons are always given in explaining the cause of those conditions-at least not all the reasons are given. In the first place the minister mentioned this afternoon-and I think it is one of the main reasons-that one of the reasons for the bad conditions out West is that the prices of agricultural products produced in the West have been deflated to a much greater extent than the prices of other products of the country. The farmer has to sell his goods at a low price but everything which he has to buy is still very much above the pre-war level. Before the war the farmers of the prairie provinces were doing fairly well in fact a very large proportion of them were doing very well, on prices very much akin to the prices of agricultural products to-day but the prices of the things they bought were very much more reasonable than those they have to pay to-day. Then the minister also mentioned what I have had pointed out to me many times by those who have lived in the West that there has been a great deal of land speculation by those who got high prices for their grain during the war years and who forgot as many of our industrialists forgot that' these prices would not prevail permanently. They speculated in land as many of us in the cities did. I know many cities west of the Great Lakes where live men who were rich are now poor. They speculated on the possibility of prices continuing high. Farmers speculated in land on the possibility of the price of grain continuing high, and to-day they find they cannot sell their products at sufficient prices to pay interest on those speculations.
But there are two other conditions that are rarely .mentioned in this House. In fact I have never heard them mentioned, although no doubt they have been without my noticing

Supply-Immigration
it. One of these factors is world conditions. Previous to the war a large proportion of our western grain was sold in Europe. Unfortunately owing to the chaotic conditions brought about by war the people of Europe are no longer able to buy our products in the same proportion as they did in pre-war days. That has been a very important factor in placing the farmers of the prairie provinces in a difficult position, and until these world conditions improve those farmers will probably remain in at least not as good a position as they were before the war. I notice by the press that Russia is again beginning to ship wheat to some of the European countries. Well, if Russia and Roumania come into the market to the extent they did before the war, it will be one more reason why the farmers of western Canada will have to take more of the advice offered them by the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) in his speech a few minutes ago, as to mixed farming for example.
If conditions are as the hon. member states, how is it going to help us in Canada to bring in more farmers to produce more agricultural products to get rid of?

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to offer advice to hon. members from the West. I leave that to my hon. friend, the leader of the Progressives. He offered some suggestions which I think might well bear investigation by most of my hon. friends who surround him. But at any rate I submit that I have offered reasons why I do not believe these millions of acres of our lands should be permitted to go to waste. I think there is room for millions of people from Europe to make a living out here even if they do not sell their products in the European markets.
What are we going to do with those products if we do not sell them in European markets?

If my hon. friend will have a little patience I may offer some suggestions and indicate what my opinions are in that respect. I was going to offer another suggestion, Mr. Chairman, in regard to a further cause of present conditions in the West. It is rarely mentioned by my hon. friends to my left. One of the main causes I think for the difficulties not only of the prairie farmers but of many farmers in other parts of the Dominion, and certainly of the farmers in my section, is that there is a practical embargo put up by the United States against the entrance of our agricultural products. I may mention in passing that the exodus to the
United States is not to a free trade country, it is to a country which to-day probably has the highest protective tariff in the world.
Will the hon. gentleman not admit that the United States to-day is the largest free 'trade area in the world.

No, Mr. Chairman, I will not admit that the United States is a free trade area at all. It is an absolutely protected area. The United States has the highest protection to-day of any country in the world. I understand what my hon. friend is pointing out.
It has free trade within its boundaries.

But Canada has a larger area than the United States, so we have a fairly large free trade area here, if it gets down to that. But at any rate the tariff barriers on goods entering the United States * are very high, and therefore I do not think anyone who wishes to be fair will argue that the United States is a free trade country. It is as Germany was before the war, a very highly protected country.
Now, Mr. Chairman, like my hon. friend, the leader of the Progressives, I have not risen with any desire to offer unfair criticisms, and I have done all the criticizing I intend to do. I wish simply to offer a few suggestions that may be of some assistance to the minister in dealing with this question.
In regard to the exodus from this country, it has been said-the minister says the figures are too great-that it amounts to something like 10,000 per month. I assume it is difficult to get accurate figures; at any rate we all admit that the exodus is very considerable. It may be of interest to the House to know that there is a very heavy exodus from the United States at the present time. Some figures I got from the Bureau of Statistics the other day show that from 1910 to 1920 the number of immigrants going into the United States was 9,000,000, while the number of emigrants going from the United States was 6,500,000, so that out of the 9,000,000 going in in that ten years, only 2,500,000 remained.
Can my hon. friend say where the emigrants from the United States went?
I have the figures, but I have not the time to look them up.

Do the countries to which they go maintain less tariff
Supply-Immigration

protection than the country whence they came?

There is only one free
trade country in the world-Great Britain; and I am sure they did not go there.
Some of them went to the war, perhaps.

Yes, and there was some exodus from Canada also on account of the war. I am certain that all those who left the United States went to protectionist countries. Certainly very few of them went back to Great Britain. I notice that there are more immigrants going into the United States from Great Britain to-day than are going into all the British dominions combined from Great Britain; so that the United States is getting quite a number from that country. I assume that most hon. members have had an oppor-. tunity of seeing the figures; it is stated that something like 75,000 are to be allowed into the United States this year from Great Britain under their rule of admission, and that that figure will be overtaken so rapidly that during the remaining eight or nine months of this year probably no more will be permitted to enter who come from Great Britain. So that the free trade of Great Britain is apparently not helping very much to hold her people within her own borders.
Can the hon. member tell me whether the United States has sought any of this immigration from Great Britain? Is she carrying on immigration propaganda in Great Britain?

I do not believe she is. I think the United States is discouraging immigration at the present time.
Now, I was suggesting some points in connection with the exodus from this country. One suggestion I wish to offer is that we should endeavour to remedy the conditions in the prairie provinces which are unjust. Judging by the questions put by some of my hon. friends, one might get the impression that I am unfriendly to the prairie provinces. I may point out to them that the whole future of my section of the country depends on the prairie provinces, so that I have every reason to be friendly to them. I have nothing but the best wishes for them and am ready to do everything I can to assist them.
All right; will the hon. gentleman offer to help us to secure a lower tariff.

I will deal with that question in a few moments, if my hon. friend will

just be patient. I marked down on my notes the word "tariff," because I knew it would come in some time.
I was going on to say that there are many injustices from which the prairie farmers are suffering, such as high railway and shipping rates. A committee of this House is dealing with shipping rates, and another is dealing with agricultural problems and the grain trade. My home city probably handles more grain at the present - time than any other city in the world. I noticed recently that Montreal was given credit for handling more grain than any other port in America; I think the figures given for Montreal were something like 125,000,000 bushels last year. But Port Arthur and Fort William, which are really one port, handled last year considerably over 200,000,000 bushels of wheat. So that this is really the greatest grain port on the North American continent-with all due respect to our good friends from Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Which is the better, Fort William or Port Arthur?

Modesty prevents my saying which. Despite the fact that Fort William is so largely dependent upon the grain trade, I believe that there are injustices in connection with that trade from which the prairie farmers are suffering. The injustices to any individual farmer may not be very great, but in the handling of the wheat generally for the whole of the prairie provinces, taking it by and large, it means a good
9 p.m. deal. I shall be pleased to see any of' these injustices wiped out. If the committee which is dealing with the banking affairs of this country can show how banking rates for the prairie farmers can be lowered, I shall be only too happy to back up any legislation looking to that end. The hon. minister this afternoon said that the farmers of the West were paying high rates of interest; I do not know whether it was he or somebody else who mentioned the payment of 9 to 10 per cent on occasions. Somebody expressed the view that 6 per cent should be a fair rate. Well, I know that the lowest rate allowed by the banks in Fort William on gilt edge securities is 7 per cent, and if the farmers of the West received their money at 7 per cent they would probably be fairly well satisfied. However, whatever we do respecting our banking institutions we cannot afford to put them in a precarious position. The whole House will stand back of the farmers, though, in any legislation which may be brought down designed to benefit them. I mention these things only to show-and I know I am speaking for the whole of this comer of the

Supply-Immigration
House-that we would do anything in our power to improve the conditions of the western farmer. .	'
There is another way in which conditions can be improved, and that is by building up the home market.
Oh, oh.

All hon. members know that the farmers of the United States sell over 90 per cent of their products in their own markets. My hon. friends to my left may laugh at the idea of building up a home market. I quite understand that it would take some time to build up a home market in Canada big enough to absorb all the grain produced in the West, but perhaps the fanners in the vicinity of Montreal, Sherbrooke, Hamilton and Toronto would not be so ready to laugh at the suggestion that we should build up a home market. I am ready to say that tariff reductions may be made that will improve conditions for the farmers, and I will answer my hon. friend (Mr. Garland, Bow River) now: I am quite agreeable to tariff reductions being made so long as he can prove that they will improve the conditions * for the farmer in the West without ruining the rest of the country. There is no doubt that free trade, which is advocated by many, would benefit the prairie provinces for a time, but it would ruin the eastern sections of the country. I cannot see that it would be advantageous to our country as a whole to ruin the East in order to benefit the West.
What about ruining the West for the sake of the East?

Well, before the war,
tariffs were not ruining the West; the West was getting along fairly well, and as soon as the conditions respecting prices, particularly of eastern products, get back where they should be, the farmers of the West will prosper; there will be no ruining of the East to help out the West or vice versa. I believe that a moderate tariff policy is what we should have in this country.
To my mind this country requires three classes of immigrants. The most important class, probably, is the farming class, consisting of men who go on the land, whether in the prairie provinces, in northern Ontario or elsewhere. I believe it would be a very good idea for this government to take into account the fact that that chasm between the East and West, extending practically from where we sit to-night to the Manitoba boundary, should be given more attention, and even if these lands are uncleared lands I believe the minister would be well advised, in the interest of
Canada as a whole and in the interest of the better understanding in this country, if he would co-operate with whatever government is in power in the province of Ontario next year and do everything he can to fill up those northern lands.
In addition to agriculturists there are two other classes that I think we need in this country. First we: need domestic servants. I believe that this country could stand to-day- to the good of Canada and the good of the people brought out for that purpose-quite a large inflow of domestic servants. There is one other class. Despite any resolutions passed by labour unions, I believe we require a certain group of labourers, particularly those who wield the pick and shovel. The Canadian will not do the work that used to be done by fhe Italian labourer, neither will the American or British immigrant. He does not wish to do that rough work. He prefers to do something a little more genteel, if I may use that expression without disrespect to the men concerned. We require in this country a certain group of immigrants who will do that work.
I have endeavoured to offer a few sugestions to the minister with the object of rendering him whatever assistance I dan. I hope he may be very successful in bringing more people to this country than he has brought in the past, and that he may have success to a greater extent than he has hitherto had in preventing people from leaving this country and going to other lands.

Mr. Chairman, Canada is, to-day, pre-eminently a land of peace and mutual respect; it is the beacon-light towards which the European nations anxious to emigrate, now turn their troubled souls to begin life anew, an ideal life which would be as the image of their former happiness. Our country enjoys complete unity, with its two dominating races whose national aspirations are similar; it is the land of religious and constitutional freedom. Although it has nine provinces, Canada has but one flag: the Union Jack. The maple leaf and the beaver are the only emblems of our country. Its soil is fertile, its forests extensive, numerous are its natural resources, its industries most promising notwithstanding these difficult after war times. However, we fully realize that an agricultural, commercial and industrial crisis is still being felt here as in other foreign countries. Trade has not yet fully recovered: it lacks stability; workmen are even forced to remain idle two or three days per week. The farmer calls loudly for markets. In short all seem to bear witness to the fact that, at
Supply-I mmigra tion

the present time, throughout Canada, our population is able to cope with the requirements of trade and industry and so contribute to their success.
The government, in which I have absolute faith and particularly the Minister of the Interior, who is competent in such matters, seem to have drawn up a wise policy on immigration though couched in rather cautious language. Let us hope that the carrying out of these ideas will have all the good effects intended, for the welfare of our people and the success of the work which they desire to place to their credit. Let us be prudent. Let us choose our immigrants with a view not only to securing the best, but also to securing the kind most needed. If we wish for the future and forever to maintain our country great and prosperous, we should strive to preserve it such as it is to-day, respectful of its forefathers' traditions and watchful of our customs and manners. With that aim in view, Mr. Chairman, we need at least immigrants who understand our economic situation and our ways, they must have sufficient intelligence and judgment to adopt, conform and especially assimilate themselves to these conditions. I do not hesitate for a moment to state on the floor of the House that Canada is in no need, at present, of labour immigration. Our national-I want to say, so as to be better understood our Canadian artisans- have a first claim to any manual and industrial employment available. We must not, by all means, bring them in contact on our own soil with the competition of foreign labour. It would be unjust at the present moment, especially in these after war hard times, when they have to toil and make the most of every opportunity so as to enable them to procure the bare necessities for themselves and their families. If agriculture needs help let us find it only in a sound and fit immigration. Let it be strictly limited to agriculture. This step would be of a practical nature, benefiting all the people in the Dominion.
The figures cited by the hon. Minister of the Interior bearing witness to the emigration of our people towards the United States, is food for thought; it is the present generation, the hope, the living and tangible future of our country which is flowing out. A repatriation policy is necessary. We must reach them either through lectures or agents, in fact by all possible -means; we must convince them that it is necessary they return to the land of their forefathers, the soil they deserted on the spur of the moment, enthused at the prospect of joining the American Republic and obtaining higher wages. If they left, naturally
[Mr. MercierJ
it is through the soliciting of others who had preceded them to that foreign land. The example was fatal. Branches were detached from the great Canadian tree; impoverished in sap the small branch found its way to the neighbouring republic, only to linger and die within a few years.
Let the Dominion government closely associate itself to the various provincial associations and adopt a common policy so that this repatriation work may bear fruit. May it bring back to our country excellent families of farmers and labourers who should never have emigrated in a passing moment of disillusion.
All the provinces suffer from the emigration of our people to the United States. The present situation resembles somewhat that of 1896. Most of the hon. members of this House will remember: uneasiness was general, trade was languishing, the smoke-stacks of mills were towering but lifeless, agriculture practically without markets and prices unstable like passing clouds. In the West, settlers shifted to the United States, even a western newspaper of the time said: "That the roads leading from Manitoba to the United States were worn and broken up by the wheels of trucks of settlers deserting the West."
Their discouragement was therefore evident; they took to the road leading to their native parish or directed their steps towards the mills over the border. The Laurier government applied a remedy to the situation and, through its efficient policy, brought back prosperity to the country. Again, in 1923, we must courageously get to work. Let us develop our natural resources and induce our workmen to further promote that object. Thus we shall again see days of abundance appear in Canada. We shall then perceive that it is not a great flood of immigration which will have rebuilt us, but our own efforts alone.

I listened this afternoon with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), but I must confess, with a good deal of disappointment. We are all anxiouf for immigration if we can get it, but I have some figures here I would like to submit to the House and I think they are entirely relevant to the discussion. I have a_ little pamphlet written by Miss Whitton, who is now, I understand, secretary to the hon. minister without portfolio (Mr. Low). The title of this pamphlet is "Some aspects of the Immigration Problem," and I gather from it that during the years 1900 to 1919 this country spent nearly $20,000,000 on immigration. What results

have we secured from that very large expenditure? Take the last census period of ten years, from 1911 to 1921, we have, according to this document-and I think the figures will stand examination-lost about two and a half million people. I would like to submit to the minister and to this House that if we are going to spend $20,000,000 in twenty years, or, say S10,000,000 dn ten years-and the minister is going to ask a very much larger appropriation for the coming year-and if we are not going to be able to retain any of the immigrants we get, what is the use of spending the money?
I am anxious, and I think we are all anxious, that we should have immigrants of the proper type in this country. We have vast natural resources to develop. We have a railway system which is capable of handling the business of two or three times the present population, but I do think we ought to give some consideration to the facts which have come to our attention during the last ten or twenty years. We have spent this large amount of money. We have received, I think, during the last forty years, nearly 5,000,000 immigrants, and during the last ten years about three and a half million, but we have not kept them. We are losing our immigrants and our natural increase almost as fast as they come. Anybody who looks at the increase of population in this country during the last twenty years, or even beyond that, and figures out the natural increase and the amount of immigration that we have received, can come to only one conclusion, namely that Canada has been and is at the present time, as was mentioned the other day in this House, an immigration sieve. I dare say a great many hon. members have read that very interesting and significant article in Maclean's Magazine a few weeks ago, "Is Canada an Immigration Sieve"? We can answer that question only in the affirmative.
There is the situation that confronts us, and I want to ask the minister and this House whether there is any better prospect of getting returns from the money that it is now proposed to expend? We have not been able to retain the immigrants. We have been throwing away the money during the last 10 or 20 years. And what difference is there now? What better prospect is there at the present time of being able to retain any of the immigrants we may secure than there has been during the last 10 or 20 years? If we had any assurance that we could retain these immigrants, there would be some advantage or propriety in authorizing the expenditure, but if it is simply maintaining a large
organization for securing immigrants who rapidly emigrate to the United States, I do not think it is good business.
There is another question also which we ought to consider before any considerable expenditures are authorized for immigration purposes. The minister in his address referred to a certain type of settler which, he stated, was wanted. It is quite possible we may secure from Europe-and I think we can secure from China and Japan, at all, events-people who are prepared to accept the conditions in this country and probably stay here. Are we prepared to receive those people? Do we want people of that type in large numbers to come into this country? We had a debate last year on oriental immigration. There are many Europeans-and I am quite satisfied the members from British Columbia will admit that there are lots of orientals-who will be glad to secure an entrance into this country, and when here will stay here, and probably make good. Are we prepared to throw our doors wide open to these people? I think, without elaborating the idea any further, we must give some attention to the immigrant's quality and general outlook, when we are dealing with prospective immigrants. I remember last summer hearing Bishop Lloyd of Saskatchewan speak of some of the problems of assimilation which the people of Saskatchewan had to face, and I must admit it was an address which impressed upon me very much the need of going carefully in regard to getting into this country in large numbers people who do not speak our language, who are not familiar with our institutions and who can be assimilated only very gradually.
Will the hon. member tell me what he means by assimilation? I should like to get his definition of it in regard to the immigrants that come into this country.

What I mean by assimilation, and what I understood Bishop Lloyd to mean, was that they should become Canadian citizens, that they should be rendered capable of taking part in our public life-in our municipal, provincial and federal life-to become good citizens. That would involve, to a very large extent, learning to speak English, the establishment of schools and so on.

Or the French
language?

The French language, certainly. I think the hon. member understands what I, mean. I think, without going into the niceties of definition, that we all understand what

I simply want to draw the attention of the House to this: that a good many of our social problems-problems that I have seen in one city in Ontario that I know pretty well

have arisen out of the demand of our manufacturing industries for cheap labour irrespective of everything else. I want the committee just to keep that in mind. It is not always the best kind of labour to get in. While we may desire cheap labour for performing rough work, and while our manufacturing and other large industries may desire that kind of labour, we ought to go just a little cautiously before we give in too much to that demand.
With respect to the remark which the minister made as to western farmers starting out by acquiring too much land, I want to suggest this, that there are two purposes for which a farmer may desire more land. He may desire to speculate; he may wish to pocket the unearned increment, and I dare say that throughout our western provinces particularly, that desire has led to purchasing large tracts of land, far larger than can be worked to advantage. But there is another reason. A farmer may wish to get what might be called the economic unit for the particular type of farming in which he is engaged, and it does not follow by any means that 160 acres is the economic unit. From what I know of western farming-and, perhaps, that is not very-much-I judge that a very much larger area than that is the economic unit in western Canada.
fMr. Good.]
I think some of us must have been very much impressed by the information which we secured this afternoon in regard to the activities of the Western Canada Colonization Association. I made a note here that it was stated that they were dealing solely with those wishing to sell or purchase land, and that they have agents throughout the United States. I presume those farmers who were mentioned as desiring to leave the high-priced lands in the United States and come to Canada are, perhaps, the unconscious victims, shall I say, of the Western Canada Colonization Association? I do not wish to deal uncharitably with this organization; but it is well known, I think, that there are a number of people in Canada and, perhaps, outside of Canada, who own large tracts of land in our western provinces, who have bought that land for speculative purposes, who are holding on to it, who, in my judgment, are parasites in this country, and who should be taxed out of their unholy or immoral earnings-earnings which they hope to get at the present time or which they have already received. I venture to suggest that it is quite possible; I do not say that it is probable
Would the hon. member call a retired farmer a parasite?
I certainly do not call a retired farmer a parasite as long as he lives on his savings. I call a man a. parasite who speculates in land and who lives on other people's earnings.
Will the hon. member say that retired farmers who are living on the incomes they derive from the farms they have previously occupied, are not, in a manner, speculators?
By no means. No, I would not admit that for one moment.
Will the hon. member permit of this suggestion, that competition is the essence of what farms are going to rent for?

The hon. member has not understood my point at all, apparently, but I think there are a good many members present who have understood it. Just in that connection, I want to point out this. I have a note here that the Canada Colonization Association acts as agent for absentee vendors. These absentee vendors are the people in western Canada who have-what shall I say?-been the curse of this country, and they are the people we ought to get after. They should be ousted from the position which they occupy. I do not consider this

country is under any obligation to show them mercy, and I should like to see those earnings that I spoke of, what is called the unearned increment, appropriated by the state. That would soon cause many of our western lands to revert to the Dominion or to the provinces, as the case might be; in that way we would have free homesteads again, and some of the people whom we want to get into this country would have some of that cheap land. About the time the war stopped and there was a prospect of our sold'ers coming back,
1	remember getting a circular from some land organization operating^ I think, in Winnipeg, informing me and all others who received the circular that we should get in on the ground floor. The returned men were coming back, the circular said; they would soon be wanting land, and now there was a chance to purchase the land, and to hold it so that when the demand was great from those returned men, we would make a good profit on our money. That was the sort of bait held out to investors in this country, and I want to say frankly here that I cannot conceive of anything more iniquitous than propaganda or temptations of that sort which were publicly circulated in this country. This has been the curse of western Canada as it has been of other new territories.
In conclusion I want to make just one or two comments on the speech of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). I was rather amused at what he said about the United States being a highly protected country. I cannot quite imagine that the hon. gentleman was serious in his description of the United States, because if there is on the face of the earth any country which shows the benefits of free trade, it is the United States.

Will the hon. member
explain to the committee in what way the United States is a free trade country?

I was about to proceed to
elaborate or elucidate my point for the benefit of the hon. member. When we consider the effect of a fiscal policy upon any nation, we must consider the proportion between the internal trade and the external trade. If a country has 90 per cent external trade and 10 per cent internal trade, as some of the very small countries have, tariffs are a serious matter for that country. I think that is quite' apparent without going into the matter any further. But if a country has 90 per cent internal trade and 10 per cent external trade, a tariff is a trifling matter. If a country has only
2	per cent external trade, you can have 100 per cent duties all around, and they will have
very little effect on that country. That is the key to the situation in the United States; the external trade is small as compared with the internal trade.

What my hon. friend is
arguing is that the tariff policy in the United States is not of great importance to the United States. I have not been arguing about that at all. Surely my hon. friend will not deny that the tariff on goods coming into the United States is a highly-protective tariff.

Of course, I am quite prepared to admit that; but I am not prepared to admit that the United States' tariff is as important a factor in the industrial life of the United States as the Canadian tariff is in the industrial life of Canada.

Of course, I admit that.
That is beside the point. The hon. member said that it amused him to have me state that the United States is a highly protective country. I should like him to give some proof- he has not given it yet unless my head is thicker than I think it is-that the United States is a free trade country.
I think the discussion is altogether out of order.

Let me continue if I am in order. I took the argument of the hon. member to be that Canadians were leaving this country in order to reap the advantages to be found in a country which was highly protective.
I was pointing out that they were, not going to a free trade country.

Well, so far as the effect of the tariff is concerned, I think they are going from a country which suffers from high protection to a country which has nominally high protection but is in reality practically a free trade country, because of the very large area and the great variety of its internal resources, and because of the fact that its internal trade is large in comparison with its external trade.
The hon. member spoke also about building up the home market. I will admit that it is particularly desirable for us to build up Canada as a manufacturing country. I should like to see as great a diversification of industry in Canada as possible; and if our farmers cannot find a foreign market, as seems likely to be the case in the near if not in the distant future, for agricultural pro-, ducts, then we ought to have a big home market. I am prepared to admit all that; but I am not prepared to admit that the tariff, to which the hon. gentleman

attributes the industrial development of Canada, has been a good thing for this country from the manufacturing or the industrial point of view. I- venture this assertion, that had there never been any tariff barrier between the United States and Canada in the last fifty or sixty years, instead of Canada having between eight and nine million people there would be a population in this country to-day of 25,000,000. And I am of opinion that without such a barrier our manufacturing industries would be ever so much larger and more important than they are at present. I believe that if we could only wipe out this tariff barrier on the North American continent we would do something which would be in the very best interest of ourselves and also of the United States. I realize that I am possibly digressing rather much in this connection; but I do not think I am going any further afield than did the hon. member whose remarks I am- considering.
Before concluding I might refer to the policy-I do not know indeed whether we can call it a policy, but at all events to the remarks-which the minister gave us this afternoon. I would be prepared to support any reasonable appropriation for an immigration organization if I could see any prospect of holding the people when we got them. The only way I can see of an immigration policy being successful judging from past experience is for us to invite the Japanese and Chinese to come in. We can hold them, and I think we can increase the population of Canada if we invite the orientals including also the Hindus.
Could you hold them on the farms?
Yes; and I think from the experience of British Columbia they would readily take to farming.
Our constituency would not have them; you are welcome to them.

I am not advocating their admission; I am simply saying that if it is only numbers that we want that is the way we can increase our population, and I do not think we should have to spend 83,000,000 a year in order to get such people. That is all I have to say at the moment on this subject.
Mr. MARI.ER: It has been a great pleasure .to listen to the discussion so far as it has gone. It reveals courage in many ways. The minister came forward with a frank and free expression as to what his policy was; the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke)

was equally courageous and I must also congratulate my fellow member from Fort William (Mr. Manion) on the manner in which he approached the situation. I am sorry that the last speaker (Mr Good) seems to think that the only kind of people whom we can keep in this couiffi'5'; are Japanese and Chin-nese. Such an attitude does seem to me to lack courage. If there was ever a time when we needed courage and vigour in connection with an immigration policy in this country, that time is the present, because if we do not put into force a bigger immigration policy and obtain more people our lifeblood will simply be drained away and we shall cease entirely to exist as a people. I offer that opinion for what it is worth, but I have no hesitation in making that statement on the floor of this House. I must admit that I am a little disappointed in the estimates; they do not go far enough. This year the estimates in this department are 81,300,000 more than they were last year, and that increase is divided under two heads, one of $600,000 in connection with the Empire Settlement Act, and the other of $700,000 for general purposes. The Empire Settlement Act I will take up at a later date. But these figures mean that the minister brings forward an increase of $700,000 for all other purposes, such as advertising, organization and matters of that description. Now; an immigration policy cannot be built up in one day. It is quite correct, as the minister states, that even if we had a perfect organization to-day we could not expect in one year or in any such short period to obtain a lot of immigrants at first hand. The organization will have to be in existence if in the future we hope to get any very large number of immigrants. For that reason I should have liked to see the minister bring down to the House a larger appropriation for this purpose, and I believe the House would have supported him in view of the urgent necessity there is for immigrants in this country. That may seem to certain hon. members to-night a peculiar statement to make; it may seem strange for me to advocate the spending of more public money in view of the finances of the country. But we should bear in mind that if this country is good it must go ahead. And it is good. It has been fought for once, and I see no reason why we should not fight for its economic existence now. And the only way I can see of fighting for that existence is to get more people to come in and produce in greater quantities from our natural resources which we have in such great abundance.

Regardless of conditions for settlement in this country?

I do not know what my hon. friend means by existing conditions; but I do not think existing conditions are as bad as he paints them.
I wish the hon. gentleman lived in my constituency. Then he would know that conditions are worse than I paint them.

I am very sorry indeed to hear my hon. friend is having such a very hard time in his constituency. If he will have a little patience with what I have to say I think he will agree with me that if we can have more production the conditions in his constituency will get considerably better.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the manner in which we are taxed and the extent is getting perfectly
appalling to all of us. If we realize that in 1914 our taxation was slightly over $21 per head of population, as against over $42 per head in 1922, in addition to which in the last few years we have advanced to the railways over .$250,000,000-
Does that include the municipal, provincial and Dominion taxation' per capita?

No, it is simply Dominion taxation. The figures are taken from the Dominion statistics. During the fiscal year 1921-22 we collected taxes to the extent of $49.43 per head of population, and yet we went behind to the tune of $92,000,000, and in 1922 we added another $80,000,000 to our national debt. In 1923 the Main Estimates call for an expenditure of over $466,000,000. It therefore means that as we are going on at the present time our taxation cannot be reduced. I do not intend to discuss finance at any great length, that is not my purpose at all, but I do think that these figures are sufficiently impressive to make us pause and think whether or not we can keep on pyramiding our national debt in this manner. I repeat that these are figures which should make any sane man who cares for the position of this country pause for a considerable time and wonder how long we can continue piling up these deficits year after year before we break.
But we are doing more than that. We are not only piling up deficits during our lifetime and it is no fault of our ministers of finance, past and present, that we are piling up these deficits, for these gentlemen have done their work well, they have done everything they possibly could for their country during their respective tenures of office-I say we are not only piling up deficits during our lifetime and are taxed out of all the de-hghts of life to the point of misery, but in addition we are handing down to the generations that shall come after us a tremendous

Give him a chance.

Was that external or internal trade?

Not external trade; simply exports plus imports.
If we turn back to the history of our own country we shall also find that during active periods of immigration trade was at its best. Take our immigration figures from 1903 to 1914.

In that 'period there entered this country nearly 3,000,000 people, to be exact 2,789,484. During that time our trade increased from $450,000,000 to $1,074,000,000. It seems to me that the objection some have to getting immigrants is not well founded, because these figures indicate that during a period of immigration trade increases very materially. That was the effect of immigration in the United States. There are really two aspects of the value of an immigrant who lands in this country; there is his ordinary value as an addition to the country and there is his value as a potential producer. In other words, every immigrant who lands on our shores at once creates trade. That was very clearly shown during the _ great immigration period of our country of which I have spoken, and the same thing happened in the United States. In that connection I was interested in an article by Mr. H. A. Hill, who at one time was secretary of the National Board of Trade of the United States. Referring to the increase of immigration there, he said:
The total immigration of 1873, as we have seen, was 422,545. The net immigration for the first half of the current year at the two principal ports of the country, so far as the returns have been accessible, proves to have been only 13,905.
He goes on to say that the immigration at that particular time would be only 100,000 for the year; then he continues:
Such a falling off in the great army of producers and consumers which has been wont to land upon our shores, while it forcibly illustrates the severity of the industrial depression through which we are passing, represents also a most serious loss to the aggregate national wealth. If, as Dr. Young estimates, the capitalized value of an immigrant on the average is $800, this loss reaches apparently the enormous sum of $240,000,000. Actually, however, large numbers of people will ultimately come hither, who are at present deterred by the unfavourable accounts.
When an immigrant lands on our shores, then, he is of particular value to the country, and that value increases. He becomes established; he starts to produce. I am not saying that we bring immigrants here simply to place a load of taxation on them; I do not look at the matter from that point of view. What I say is this: the more we get out of the soil the more we increase the natural wealth of the country and enable those who are here and those who come here to assume their fair share of taxation.

The hon. gentleman is arguing that every immigrant that we bring into the country increases our wealth. Would that apply to other countries, and why are other countries anxious* to get rid of their people?

Are those other countries anxious to get rid of their people?
The hon. member must know that several European countries are very anxious to get rid of some of their people. England, for that matter, has an appropriation for that very purpose.

It is true that England does want to send out some of her people because England is an
10 p.m. over-populated country, and the same applies to many other countries across the seas. But we are not over-populated here. We have millions of acres of land; we have natural resources that we cannot use, and every man who has a pair of hands, a good heart and sound brain can enrich this country by getting the natural resources out of the soil. To leave those natural resources as they are makes them worthless to us or anyone else. It is manpower we want; we must get our wealth out of the soil-because the wealth does come out of the soil in one way or another.

Will that man who goes on
the soil be enriching this country any if he gets less than the cost of production for what he produces?

That question cannot be answered in two words, and if the hon. member will permit me I shall be glad to answer it later in the course of my remarks.
I was going to show the value of the immigrant to our country. Take our internal trade. I think it was stated in this House last year that the Dominion Statistician had reported that the value of Canada's production in 1921 was estimated at over $5,000,000,000 and that the total production plus the imports but minus the exports represented the value of our internal trade. In 1921 our imports were valued at about $30,000,000 more than our exports, so that according to this calculation our internal trade was valued at $5,200,000,000, or $600 per head of population. I claim that every man who comes into this country will increase that internal trade, and the result wall be an acceleration of the work of our factories and a demand for all our farm products. In that way the unemployment which at present exists will be largely done away with.
The hon. gentleman means, I suppose, every man we can keep in this country.

I am coming to that question also, if my hon. friend will permit me. I do not want to quote the newspapers regarding the necessity of immigration, but there are just one or two comments to which I wish to direct attention. I shall not quote entirely from the eastern press, because I have been told that the eastern press is prejudiced to a certain extent. But let me quote one remark made to the meeting of the National Trust Company. That company has a great many interests in the West, and I believe it is one of the best posted companies in the Dominion. The president of the National Trust Company says:
I wish to-day to again emphasize this question. Immigration, it seems to me, stands in the forefront of the important problems facing our country at the present time. I feel confident there is no other single factor which would contribute so much to the solution of all our problems, and in the end to the material comfort and contentment of every class in Canada. There exists to-day upon our farms and in several of our industries a demand for labour which cannot be filled. The cry against unmigration, when examined, is found lacking in substance. Immigration properly controlled and well directed will injure none, but must benefit all. What we need in this Dominion is volume of business. This is strikingly illustrated in our railway situation. We have a large equipment in every business activity-too large for the needs of our present population. More people would create greater demands upon our equipment and thus afford a larger market for labour, for agriculture, for manufacturers and for all.
There may be some hon. members who will not agree with what the president of the National Trust Company says-I hear one hon. gentleman say "hear, hear"-but it does seem to me that, generally speaking, his remarks are characterized by a good deal of sense. The member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) speak. ing at Winnipeg on the 10th of November, said:
Canada has a hard way ahead of it. The surest guarantee of our future prosperity lies in the wise development of our agricultural resources.
The western members will probably agree with that.
"Wise development".
Wise development, that is right.
How are you going to have development of our agricultural lands unless you get men able to develop them.'
Make it profitable for them to do so.

Premier John Bracken apparently does not take that view. This is what he said, speaking in the Manitoba legislature on the 31st of last January:

He continues:
Many thought these two things were antagonistic. He did not regard them as that. He believed they were complementary and went hand in hand. The government would do all it could to improve agricultural conditions and, at the same time try to bring into the country a reasonable amount of good settlers.
Now, that I think from the Premier of the province of Manitoba is perfectly clear. And in the London Times which is a veyy well informed paper and has correspondents all through Canada-
Did the Premier of Manitoba say that he would limit these immigrants to one class only?
I do not know whether he said that or not. Does my hon. friend say he did say that?
No, I was just hoping that he did not say it; I did not know what he said.
I do not know. I cannot read what the mind of Premier John Bracken said, I can only, unfortunately, read what he is reported in the newspaper to have said.
Did the Premier at that time mention that the people of Manitoba owed taxes over $14,000,000?

No, I do not think he did. I was going on to read what the London Times said about the necessity of immigration to Canada. It said on the 4th September,
' 1922:
What Canada needs more than anything else is population. She needs a strong immigration policy, together with the widest possible advertisement of what she 'has to offer. Her empty spaces are calling for settlers. She has less than three people to the-square mile, whereas her neighbour across the border has thirty-five, and the Japanese across the Pacific have more than three hundred.
The Japanese my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good) spoke about.
Now, what I would like to make quite clear to the committee to-night is that in the first place I believe the only way we can produce is by means of having more man power in this country; that unless we do produce more we

cannot lighten the load of taxation which this country is suffering under at the present time.
The question will naturally arise in the minds of all those I am addressing to-night, what kind of immigrant should be brought into this country? In other words, am I in favour of deluging the country with anybody who may come in? Should we go after that class of immigrant, or should we have another kind of immigration policy in Canada? The policy that I am in favour of comprises two classes of immigrants. The first I call, for want of a better name, "A preferred class of immigrant". Those are the immigrants which, in my opinion, we should go after. Those are the immigrants we should spend our money to bring to this country and when we get them-and I will speak of that later on- keep them here. Another class of immigrant is the immigrant who presents himself at our doors, and if people voluntarily present themselves at our doors and ask to come into the country I do not think they should be refused admittance. In other words I claim this: There is ample work for everybody in this country who is willing and anxious to work. Perhaps there is not ample work for those who are not willing and anxious to work, but I would not close the door in the face of any immigrant who was sound in body and mind and came to the doors of this country and asked to be admitted.
Does the hon. member include the orientals in that?
No, I am not speaking of oriental immigration at all; that is entirely out of my mind.

Would the hon.
gentleman suggest that something like 6,000 people who are being kept by the city of Winnipeg are not able and willing to work? The same thing is true of other cities in this country.

I do not want to hurt my
hon. friend's feelings in any way.

There is no danger of hurting my feelings. I asked a simple question of the hon. gentleman, whether he means to imply that the large number of unemployed men in the cities of Canada are unwilling to work.

I do not mean to be at all impertinent in replying to my hon. friend. Whether they are willing to work or not what I say is this: I believe the great majority of

Sa-pply-Immigration
those men could get work if they went out and looked for it.

What
would they get employment at during the last two years if they went out to look for it?
Farm labour.

I was going to deal with
the question of unemployment in Canada later on.
I have asked the hon. member a fair question and I would like to get a fair answer. I do not believe in putting a matter off until later in the evening in order to avoid answering a question.
