speechtext:
Order. The
hon member who is speaking may answer the question if he so desires. If he does not desire to answer he is not compelled to do so.

I will answer my hon.
friend's question with pleasure. From all that -I can read-I may not have the distinct knowledge that my hon. friend has of certain conditions-it does seem to me that the question of unemployment in this country is not as serious as has been pointed out. My knowledge is derived entirely from the press of the country. The knowledge I have acquired in that way may be quite wrong; I would be very glad to be corrected if that is the case. But here is a clipping from the Toronto Saturday Night, of 28th October, 1922, which I intended to read in any event:
In many centres in Canada, if not in all, there Is a distinct shortage of labour in certain activities. This is specially apparent in the building trades. All through the spring and summer there have not been sufficient masons, carpenters, bricklayers and plasterers to meet the demand, and in consequence building operations have been held up. Structures which in the old days would have been fully completed in that period between April and November are still, roughly speaking, half done.
That is one report which I read. Another report which I read was taken from the Financial Post of the 16th February, 1923. Dealing with the New Brunswick labour situation, the lumber cut, the article says:
The lumber cut in New Brunswick for this winter is expected to exceed that of any winter for the past five years. There have been two drawbacks to a large clJf too much snow in the woods and a dearth of men. In many of the sections so much snow has fallen that cutting concerns have been unable to use horses, in fact conditions have become so acute that several companies have ceased operations.
Regarding the scarcity of men in Now Brunswick, the cause is migration to other provinces and to New England.
There is a further clipping that I read some little time ago-now we go farther west- from the Financial Post of the 16th February, 1919.

Does the article state
where the men from New Brunswick went to? I think if it does he will find they have gone over to the states of Maine and Massachusetts.

No not all of them. I
would be glad to continue reading the quotation if the hon. member so desires. Some of them did go there.
Regarding the scarcity of men in New Brunswick, the cause is the migration to other provinces and to New England.
That is as far as I read. Now to continue-
The American government has allowed two thousand lumber-jacks to be imported into New England from New Brunswick, owing to the scarcity of men in New England. Originally the two thousand men were turned back at the border by the United States immigration agents but on the appeal from lumber companies in Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont operations, the United States labor department lifted the bars.
In addition to the two thousand that went to the New England woods, ten thousand men have gone to the woods of Quebec and Ontario.
I was going to speak of British Columbia:
In spite of warnings issued last fall that the present winter would witness unemployment in British Columbia on a scale greater than ever experienced, there is today very little idle labour in the province. At some points the demand for workers has been so great that men have been brought in from Alberta and Saskatchewan. This was notably the case in connection with the tie cutting operations along the line of the Canadian National railway east of Prince Albert. Logging operations in the interior have been held up by heavy snow-fall, but that is a purely temporary condition, and on the coast the logging concerns are operating at full strength.
I spoke about the situation in New Brunswick and I referred to the situation in Toronto and in British Columbia. I have given this information for what it is worth and I have taken information from the only source from which the average man obtains his information. Take the city of Montreal, the actual situation there is not as serious as has been alleged. Of course there is some unemployment there, but I have had no difficulty in my little experience in placing men who came to me asking for jobs. I have answered the question the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) to the best of my ability. That is the general situation as I see it.

I do not want to press this matter unduly, but I say that resolutions passed in the city of Winnipeg have been placed before this House, calling attention to the thousands of people in that city who have been out of work and are to-day out of work.
Supply-Immigra tio n

I have information from the mayor of the city that the situation is very serious. Reference has been made to British Columbia. I know the conditions there very intimately, and men who were employed there two years ago have gone to the woods on the other side in thousands. Is that not so?

I do not know whether my [DOT] hon. friend will admit the correctness or incorrectness of these reports. Most of them are written in Toronto-a very reputable city as I have heard-and I have almost taken them as being absolutely correct. I do not deny what the hon. member says about the Winnipeg situation. I do not wish the hon. member to misunderstand me. I have no antipathy towards labour-quite the contrary

but I have asserted that I do think, that, in many cases, certain classes of labourers at the present time do not like difficult labour and they will not accept employment where the work is hard. If they would do so I think most of the labourers would be employed. That is the viewpoint I take. I have no disrespect for labour-quite the contrary.
I was going on to speak in regard to the class of immigrants we need in this country.
I stated that in my opinion there were two classes so-called. The first was the class that we spoke of as the agriculturist; the man who would be placed on the land. I also said -and I would like to repeat-so that the trend of my thoughts will be continuous-that we should not close the doors to other immigrants coming to this country, but if they are strong and healthy and willing to work they should be allowed to come in. In addition to that, I would like to say, even if it is digressing at the present time, that I think that those who have relatives abroad in various parts of Europe should be allowed to bring those relatives into this country, and that certain restrictions,, existing at the present time should be removed.
However, I would like to go back and explain why, in my opinion, the agriculturist is required at the present time. It appears to me that in any country we require to have a properly balanced population. If you have a larger urban population than rural population, it is ill-balanced. The rural population is tributary to the urban population. At the present time in this country our population is not properly balanced, and the rural population has in many cases gone down in percentage during the past twenty years. Take the figures for the whole of Canada, and we find that in 1901 the rural population was 62i per cent, and in 1911 it was 54.58 per cent. In 1921 it was 50.47 per cent. In other words,

the rural and urban populations are pretty nearly equal. Some hon. member will say that the reason they are so nearly balanced is because it does not pay to farm. That may or may not be the case, but I think there are other reasons why the rural population is not increasing as it should. But whether it is increasing or not the reason that I suggested a moment ago that it is decreasing on account of the farm not paying is no reason in the wide world why we should not have courage enough to bring out to this country agriculturists and place them on the land, because they are certainly needed there in order to increase production. I am not in favour of urging a great influx into our cities, but I do urge that we should bring forward as many agriculturists as we possibly -can and place them on the land.
We always imagined, from our past immigration figures, that the great majority of the immigrants who came here went on the land. That is not the case. They did not, at least, go to the western provinces where we thought they were going:	In the last 20 years for
example, 51 per cent of the immigrants went to the Maritime provinces, Quebec and Ontario, and less than 50 per cent went to the West. Although I have urged the government at the present time to bring out agriculturists, there is no use bringing these people out and landing them in Winnipeg or some western city and not actually placing them on the farm and looking after them. We should bring them here, not as strangers, but as future citizens of Canada, and make them understand that this is to be their home. There is at the present time an excellent organization called the Soldier Settlement Board which can look after immigrants who come here. They are able not only to bring immigrants to the proper sections of the country on which they can be placed but they can explain to them what should be grown and what should not be grown. They can keep a watchful eye over the immigrant when he comes here, during his early years in Canada, and, generally speaking, the Soldier Settlement is a most excellent organization in every way, and the man at the head of it is a thoroughly reliable and able man. The Soldier Settlement Board has done remarkably well in this country in every way. Some people are very apt to say that the land which was bought for the soldiers has been a loss. There has not been a loss on that land. There has been a certain loss, I admit, on the stock and implements, but as regards land purchased for the soldiers up to 31st January last there was a surplus-I am speaking of

Supply-Immigration
the lands taken back-of over $402,000 what was paid for the lands then.
Does this include what the soldier himself paid as his initial payment and his subsequent payments, or just what the government put in?
If the hon. member had asked me that question last year I could have answered it, but I cannot answer it now.
I am inclined to think it does not.
I am inclined to think it does include what the soldier put in. The hon. member does not think so?
No.

I am not competent to say whether it does or not. I would like to repeat, without wearying the House, my statement that the government should put agriculturists on the land. In addition to that, I would even go so far as to be in favour of a scheme of colonizing certain parts of this country, where the farms may be too large, by bringing people in, dividing up the farms, and letting the newcomers cultivate parts of these farms, even if the government had to set aside a certain amount of money for this purpose. I know perfectly well the minister does not approve that method, but if colon, ists were brought in and these farms divided up, it would not only help the colonist coming in, but it would also help very many of the farmers in the northwest, who at the present time, as I am informed, are overburdened with too much land and a great deal of debt. We have also certain free lands still in the various provinces and the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) spoke about those lands to-day. He spoke of a certain class of immigrants we could bring out here. I do not think we can get all the agricultural immigrants we require from Great Britain. We will have to go to the continent of Europe for them. The question is not whether these immigrants are of a lower standard of living or not. That is a sad way to look at things. The question is whether Hungarians and people of that description are willing to go on and work and clear land of that description, when others are not willing to do it.
Is the hon. member, therefore, willing that we bring in immigrants of a lower standard of living?

I did not say that at all. I particularly attempted to avoid, in as clear a way as I could, saying that there was any desire to bring in immigrants of a lower
standard of living. I said that as regards these immigrants who could be got from Europe-I used the Hungarians as an example -the question was not whether they were satisfied with a lower standard of living, it was whether they were willing to go on land of this description, clear it and work it. There are such people scattered throughout Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta, so I am informed, who have been doing remarkably well, and there are in those countries, I presume, people of that class, who can be made to populate such lands, who, I believe, will be contented there, and who will, in course of time, become splendid citizens. That is what I referred to in speaking of bringing in immigrants ; I used the word " Hungarian " simply as an example of the class who, I believe, would be satisfactory.
Why should the manufacturers of eastern Canada not be willing to face the same kind of competition?
What kind of competition?

When the hon. member refers to bringing in those people to live under circumstances under which the present citizens cannot make it go, or make their farming pay, he is certainly advocating a system of extreme competition. He is advocating something that, if brought to its logical conclusion, means that the present settlers will have to get out or else adopt the other standard of living.

Does that whole question not some down to the fact whether farming in Canada can or cannot be made to pay?
I claim that farming can eventually be made to pay; but there are certain fundamental facts which are at the present time preventing farming from paying. I do not think there 1 is on the floor of this House any man who has greater sympathy for the West than I have, and I am coming to that point in just one moment.
Before doing so, I want to speak regarding the amount which has been placed in the Estimates to be used under the Empire settlement scheme. The minister has included in the estimates an amount of $600,000 for the purpose of paying assisted passages of men and domestic servants and various other classes of settlers. Let me make myself quite clear as regards British immigration. I would be only too glad to see as many British immigrants come to this country as we can get; but we should realize at the present time that there is a particular class of immigrant which
Supply-Immigration

we require, that is the agriculturist, and the agriculturist should be the man preferably to be helped under this particular scheme. When there are plenty of people who will come to our doors without being paid assisted passages, those assisted passages should not be meted out to the clerical class and classes of that description under the British Empire settlement scheme. In other words, if labour is required in any particular locality, by all means help to bring out that labour. If labour can be supplied by the Canadian people themselves, we should not assist labour to come out to Canada by means of paying assisted passages. But we should pay assisted passages where the immigration officer knows there is a good farmer or a good farming family desirous of coming out to Canada for the purpose of farming. I repeat again; I am not opposed to British immigration, rather the contrary.
I wish to say just a word as regards the orders in council which are at present in force, and I hope the government will, in the course of a short time, take into consideration the question of cancelling those orders in council. No doubt they were passed at a time when it was necessary to make them, but now their usefulness has very largely passed. I cannot myself see the necessity of the non-continuous journey order in council. I cannot see the great necessity either of the alien enemy order in council.
Mr. MeBRIDE: If the order in council in connection with the non-continuous journey had not been passed, would not the western part of this country have been flooded with Hindus?

Let us face the situation like men. If we do not want Hindus in this country let us say so; but do not let us pass an order in council that blankets everybody else and says to a man coming from the United States or any other place from which we welcome immigrants: "No, you cannot come in here, simply because you have not come by a continuous journey." If we do not want Hindus or any other class of people, let us say so; but do not let us pass a blanket order in council and keep it in force.
I was going to say a few words about the alien enemy order in council. Various hon. members may have feelings on that subject. Some of us may think we should not allow into this country those who have been connected with countries which were at war with Great Britain or her allies during the great war. I know there are mixed feelings on that subject, and perhaps I am treading on very dangerous ground in speaking about the

matter at all. But I do not think we should continue to foster and keep up this war feeling any longer in this country. We should recognize that we have a great big country to fill up, a country rich in natural resources, and although I am not in favour of flooding any one particular section of Canada with people from any particular part of Europe, putting them in a community and saying: "You can have your own laws, your own schools and half a dozen other things," I am in favour of a general immigration in a fair, selected and directed way from all the countries of Europe, provided that the immigrants who are brought forward are suitable. For that reason I think this alien enemy order in council should be eliminated.
The hon. member discussed the matter of the Soldier Settlement Board. Would he favour the extension of the principles of the Soldier Settlement Board to others than soldier settlers?

I am very much obliged to the hon. member for Calgary West, asking that question. Yes, I would. I am quite frank in saying that I believe the Soldier Settlement Board, if extended in other directions, would prove a great colonization agency in this country, and that the money would be very well spent if money were set aside for the purpose Of bringing people in and colonizing them and keeping them on the land. As a proof that I do not think the country would lose a single dollar by a policy of that description, I cite the splendid work that the Soldier Settlement Board have done in regard to settling returned soldiers. When they bought their land, they had not as great experience as they have now; and if they went out now and bought land of this description and put suitable families of settlers on to those lands, the money would be well spent in the interest of this country.
During the course of this debate, the question of the lure of the south was taken up time and time again. I do not think we should be so terribly afraid of the lure of the south. You will get the ebb and flow in every country of the world; you cannot prevent that. You will never be able to prevent Canadians from going to the United States or Americans from coming to Canada. You will always have that ebb and flow so long as these two great countries, with no barriers of any kind between them, exist. But we can prevent that flow into the United States to a very great extent by making this country a better country to live in, by building up this country itself, by making positions here for our young men so that our

Supply-Immigration
young men will be willing and ready to stay at home instead of going to the United States. Frankly, I do not know that one can blame an ambitious man for wanting to go to the United States now with its tremendous possibilities. As a matter of fact, one has to look around with a great deal of care and wonder what one will do with one's children when they grow up, when one sees the possibilities of this country dwindling away I believe that anyone who has faith in this country-and I have unbounded faith in the country and in its people-will agree that it is well worth while spending money on immigration to bring immigrants into Canada. But someone will say, what about the lure of the south? Well, we have also had in this country considerable immigration from the United States of America. In the period from 1900 to 1909, 403,000 such immigrants came into this country; from 1910 to 1919, 875,000 came; and in 1920, 1921 and 1922, 127,000 came in. Someone will say, however, that a great many of our people have gone to the United States. So they have. But I doubt very much whether the figures which have been repeatedly given in this House regarding those going to the United States are absolutely correct. As everyone knows, we do not keep records with regard to emigration from this country to the United States. Those records are kept by the United States officials, and in many cases in the- past they have been found to have counted as permanent settlers in the United States people who have gone there only on a temporary visit. An investigation was made by the department in two instances, in 1910 and 1912, when a large number of cases were inquired into. I am taking this from the Canadian Annual Review which I saw the other day; and out of 849 cases of persons reported as having gone to the United States to settle, it was found by actual examination that 415 had gone only on a temporary visit. The Review goes on to give the statistics of emigration from Canada to the United States and from the United States to Canada. It shows that in the period 19101914 there came from the United States to Canada 605,498 people while there went from Canada to the United States 329,000. In the period 1915-1919 the trend was not quite so favourable: 379,000 went from Canada to the United States as compared with 270,000 from the United States to Canada. But be that as it may, there is no reason in the wide world why the Canadian people should lose courage. There is no reason why we should be downhearted because a certain number of our citizens are going to the United States from .year to year. In this matter courage is all
that is required; and if we have a courageous policy, as we have a courageous people, I am confident that sooner or later we shall make this a good country to live in and shall retain not only our own people but the settlers that come in.
But when we talk to-day of Canadians going to the United States, we must realize that there are reasons for this exodus. The Dillingham law in force there, as stated this afternoon, restricts the immigration of aliens to 3 per cent of the nationals resident in the United States; that is to say, of people from the United Kingdom, only 3 per cent of the number of British people resident in the United States can enter that country, and so forth. That has made a very great shortage in labour in the United States, and now there is a tremendous building boom in Chicago and Los Angeles and I believe in Boston, although I am speaking only from, memory as regards the last-named city. If our artisans therefore find that they can get large wages in the United States they are going to go there -in large numbers. And they are going; there is no denying that, because it is the case. But because that is the situation at the present time, because our people are leaving Canada just now for specific reasons, is that any reason why we should conclude that the lure of the United States is something that will always exist? It does seem to me that in due course of time conditions will revive here and we shall be enabled to retain our population. But it will do us no good to sit down and declare that so long as there is this lure to the United States we are not going to get any people to come here. That is not going to do us a bit of good. If we take any such despondent attitude we shall simply find that more and more of our people will go to the United States, our trade will sink lower and lower, and our population will gradually eliminate itself, creating a condition that may be very unpleasant to contemplate.
Now I want to say a word as regards the attitude of certain gentlemen in the West on the question of immigration. And if I .speak personally and feelingly I think that hon. gentlemen will believe what I say. There is no man in this House who has a greater sympathy with those pioneers who went to the West than I have, for I believe they have done for this country something that no other people have accomplished. They have withstood hardships and tilled the land and reaped enormous crops. The figures of the past year of their tremendous crop, as taken from the Manitoba Free Press, show a total of 903,000,000 bushels of grain valued at the head of the lalses at $590,000,000. I know that some

Supply-Immigration
hon. gentlemen will observe that it did not pay. Well, perhaps it did not; nevertheless the men who have raised that enormous crop of grain, of such a huge value, and brought tha,'' vast area of land under cultivation, surely do not lack in courage. I am perfectly positive that they cannot lack courage, and I believe that the conditions prevailing in the West to-day are due more or less to fundamental causes which I think will be removed.
Does not the hon. gentleman think that we are entitled to a little more than commendation for our courage?

Yes, certainly. I think you are entitled to a great deal more, and you will get a great deal more too, I am perfectly sure. As I was remarking, there are fundamental reasons to-day that prevent farming from being very profitable in the West, and I approach the matter with a great deal of hesitation, I must admit. The first reason is, of course, that the farmer's dollar is worth only about 70 cents while he has to pay a great deal more for all his commodities. But the prices of commodities are going down at the present time.
What about sugar?

And when further deflation does take place it seems to me that the farmer's dollar will be worth a great deal more than it can now purchase. Another reason is that the European buying power is not what we should like it to be. It is not very good now, but I believe it will improve as time goes on; and that will make the situation still better. There is another question that we must consider, and that is the matter of freight rates, which are weighing heavily on the farming industry. I do not see how we are going to bring down freight rates unless we give the railways more. freight. It is not possible for them to reduce rates unless they can get more freight.
Did the hon. member read the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company?
Yes, in one of the Toronto papers. What about it?
You will find in that report that they made this year a net surplus of over $22,000,000. Does my hon. friend not think that we ought to have a lowering of rates in view of that fact?

The net surplus was not $22,000,000. After paying a reasonable divi-

dend on the money invested it was probably more like $1,000,000, because the Canadian Pacific Railway was running behind largely all through the year, and it was only when the fall crop came that they were able to earn dividend requirements.

May I quote the figures for the hon. gentleman's benefit? The net earnings from the railway and lake steamers was $36,301,691, and after deduction of fixed charges the surplus is given as $22,952,785.
The dividend must come out of that.

Yes. Does the hon. gentleman not want the shareholders to get anything at all? The surplus of the Canadian Pacific Railway last year, after the payment of a moderate dividend after years of patient striving, was comparatively little. However, that is a digression.
Now, I have taken up with the committee as far as I think is necessary the question of unemployment, and I have only one word to add. I should like to repeat that if we adopt a courageous immigration policy and bring in the right class of settlers it will help us along very much. Some hon. members may say, "Well, if we get more immigrants in here what are we going to do?" I would reply that if we do not take a chance and bring immigrants in our home markets will dwindle, our population will decline, and the lure of the United States will continue, thus perpetuating the conditions which we now deplore so much.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to take very much time at this hour of the night, but I would not desire to economize by omitting a reference that I think ought to be made to the very valuable address which we have just listened to. Possibly I would not associate myself with all of the hon. member's arguments nor with all of his conclusions, but I think it is to the credit of this House that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Marler) should have given bo much study to what in my mind is one of the two important questions that confront our people to-day. For in my judgment there are no more than two questions now before the country, nor are there likely to be any others for Borne years to come. One is the railway question, on which I shall not touch to-night; the other is the question of immigration. I think this committee realizes that the question which we have so often debated-the tariff-no matter how strong the views of many hon. members may be, is something that by the

Supply-Immigration
agency of any party cannot be changed by more than a fractional variation from its present condition, and therefore we may as well settle down to consideration of the great questions of railways and of immigration.
I believe the country is prepared to support the hon. Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) if his policy contains that element so much emphasized by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler)-courage. It is only by courage that this problem can be successfully handled.	I do not think the
people of Canada expect that every immigrant will remain here. If we were to take a view so limited we would not spend a dollar, we would not make a single effort to attract desirable immigrants; on the contrary, we would allow our country to wither, to die of inanition. That cannot be the Canadian spirit. Certainly it is not the spirit by which we have surmounted the difficulties of the past, and it is not the spirit which will solve our national problems to-day.
After all, immigration is like a fertilizing stream, which passes through the land depositing something of its value, but always carrying something away. We cannot expect to retain all the immigrants we bring in. It is our business to make conditions here favourable to the retention of every immigrant, and especially of every native-born son. But we cannot war against human nature. No parliament can stop that onward progress of the ambitious boys and girls from the farm to the civic centre, and thence to the greatest opportunities of life. Nor is it desirable that we should try to turn the world back. Progress is the natural order of events, and we should not desire to stop it even if we had the ability to do so. Neither is it possible for us to stop the tide of immigration flowing through to other countries. We know that the United States is greater in population, in wealth and in opportunity, and it is perhaps not a little to our credit that our native-born of ambition, of courage and of ability have left us to occupy leading positions in the country to the south; and there is no reason why we should desire to stop them. But we must replace them by attracting immigrants in increasing numbers, and therefore I think this country should be opened to a selected immigration, an immigration which ought in my judgment to be directed to the parts of the Dominion that want it and ask for it.

How can you keep that

I have just said that you
cannot stop its natural movement, you cannot cause a fixation of the human character. I have seen something that possibly resembles
an effort at fixation, but I would not want Canada to attempt it.
I do not purpose to discuss the problem of immigration from east to west and from nort to south, but to treat it from what in one sense is purely a sectional aspect. I want to speak of immigration from the standpoint of the Maritime provinces, and I think I am justified in doing so. We have heard from every other part of the Dominion its attitude towards immigration. We in the Maritime provinces have our attitude. We would like to see our desires 'translated into action. While I cannot congratulate the minister upon any particular courage in the "policy which he puts forward, nor upon any great ambition involved in that policy, still I feel that the hon. gentleman is sincere in his desire to do all he can so far as his path is clear to him, and I think whether we agree with him or not in details it ought to be the part of hon. members to give him at least such suggestions as they think are of value. He will then have the opportunity of selecting those which to him possess merit. It was largely for that purpose I am sure that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George delivered his speech. I want to make this suggestion myself, I trust that this debate, which is one of very great value to the country, will be .made up of a succession of suggestions with the view of giving the minister assistance which will enable him to make his department more helpful to the country.
Now', we have to a certain extent a complaint in the Maritime provinces in regard to immigration. I trust we are not of a whining breed and that we do not complain for the sake of complaining. I hope we have not yet come to the conclusion that the axis of Canada is in the Maritime provinces and that the rest of the Dominion must revolve around it and by our permission. We do not take any such stand, but we do intend to say what we think we need and to point out a way by which we think it can be given to us. Hitherto, no matter what government has been in power, as the minister said to-day, the policy has been to treat the Immigration department as a sort of fly on the wheel of the administration-a general sign hung out and a certain amount of money spent in a certain way to attract people. Where? To Canada. That is all right as a glittering generality.
The federal government has always refused to make distinctions between the provinces, and in that respect I think it has failed to do justice to all Canada. The result of that policy has been that people have flocked to the western lands. It is true that we have the burden of the Canadian Pacific to help to

carry, and we have the burden of the Canadian Northern. I shall not follow all the changes of name in connection with the Canadian Northern down to the present time, but we still have the burden with us, and it is quite right to get settlers into that country. But is it quite fair that there should be no direction of the stream of immigration toward other provinces which need the vitality of immigration quite as much as the West needs it? The House sees exactly what has taken place in the Maritime provinces. We have either lost population, as in the case of the beautiful little province of Prince Edward Island, or made a gain so slight that we are losing representation, as in the case of Nova Scotia, or are barely able to hold our own, as in the case of New Brunswick. That is the fact in relation to this last decade; in the previous decade we lost in our relative position to the provinces as a whole. Now, do we not need some of the immigration? Do we not want it? Are there not fertile valleys, pleasant slopes, lovely plains, in these three provinces? Are there not great natural resources which can be developed by labour? We want population, not talking machines. If other people want the country to stand still; if they do not wTant immigration; if they do not want success they can so express themselves, as they have done many times before. For my part, I will do my own talking. I am not a catechism.
Conditions in the Maritime provinces from the agricultural standpoint differ greatly from those in the West. Our soil in most instances requires to be denuded of some growth. The proposal I will make may appear startling, because it might involve the expenditure of a few hundred thousand dollars. It might even cost a million or a couple of millions. It maybe startling to gentlemen on both sides who yesterday with the greatest complacency approved of the spending of millions upon millions to complete the Hudson Bay railway. If that dream of some peoples' lives is to be realized, we in the Maritime provinces may fairly put in a plea for a chance for our own lives, and what I say is that the immigration policy could very well embrace the expenditure of some money upon a suitable class of immigrants by preparing farms for them in the Maritime provinces. If you do that, we will keep them there, and we will not whine if the crops go bad. I trust that the minister may be able to persuade his colleagues to give him enough money to enable us to

Mr. Chairman, I regret that I cannot agree with much that has been said by hon. members opposite and by the minister himself. Wre are all pretty^ well agreed that so far as the minister is concerned he at least has no immigration policy; the immigration policy that he is proposing has been handed to him by outside schemers who wish to have their plans promoted. I would have thought that the Liberal government after taking office would have seen fit to try to find out the cause of emigration from our country. This country has had problems of immigration and emigration for the past forty years. During all that time we have not maintained our natural increase in Canada, yet, we have spent millions upon millions of dollars in bringing tourists to our shores and allowing them to drift out of the country again. The minister now proposes to do something even worse; he is going to pay passages and thus assist these people to come to Canada. If the government of the day had lived up to their pre-election pledges and promises to put a certain tariff into effect in this country, they would have freed the implements of production from customs tariff. If that had been done the result would have been a great incentive in the matter of bringing people to this coimtry and making our present farming population more prosperous, more happy and more contented. That, after all, is what will bring the most immigrants to Canada and keep them here-a prosperous, happy and contented people. All the immigration propaganda that the minister talks of is not worth one cent to him; is not going to get him anywhere.
He proposes to spend $600,000 in bringing people into Canada by means of assisted immigration, and he intends to participate in the British Empire settlement scheme. Now, that scheme is designed to get rid of the surplus population of Great Britain. It is a very good scheme for the British people, but what are we to do with these people after we get them here? Put them in the cities and open soup kitchens for them? Nothing else can happen. These people are being brought from the cities of England; they are not people who wall be assimilated into the rural life of our country. They are not people who will go on the farms of northern Quebec, northern Ontario, northern Saskatchewan and Alberta. If the minister will attempt to legislate so as to make conditions in the rural districts livable for the people who are there; if he will do something to bring prosperity to the farming communities, then he will get all the immigrants that Canada wants, with very little effort on his part.

There are four things necessary for this country to-day, and one of them is tariff adjustment. We have lived under this present tariff arrangement of protection for the past forty years and we have got nowhere. Our transportation system is bleeding the people white, and it is the duty of the government to see that the people get a square deal from the transportation companies. Our banking system is so arranged that there are no rural ' credits, no provisions for the development of the rural districts. It is so arranged that the money is gathered into the cities. I am not blaming the banks; they are doing business-according to their lights, according to the best profit they can get, but under the present system the country banks are simply gathering offices for the cities. The result is that the bankers of Canada are in the large cities- Toronto and Montreal; and they are anxious to lend money to the manufacturer, the jobber and the speculator. Your money and the money of the rural districts finds its way to Montreal and is there lent out. I do not know that this condition can be remedied immediately, but it is one of the things that has helped to depopulate rural Canada. There is no person in rural Canada in a position to make loans through the banks. It is true that a private individual can make loans; but the boy in the bank in the rural districts of Canada is not competent to do so.

Now, Mr. Chairman, this waste of money in Canada has gone on too long. This system of paternalism is getting too great a hold on the Canadian people. We are not only going to bring these immigrants into
Canada but we are going to regulate their movements after they get here; we are going to have a system of inspection and of restrictions. We are going to tell these people how they are to farm, when they are to farm and why; we are going out to waste the money of the Canadian people, a thing that we cannot possibly afford to do.
My hon. friend also has a schfeme to spend $100,000 with the Canadian Colonization Company. Just imagine the federal government meddling with real estate problems! Just imagine them wasting the people's money in a real estate deal of that kind! Why if my hon. friend will spend, not $100,000 but $1,000, he will be able to stop as many people from leaving Canada in a week or in a day as his agreement requires to be brought in in a year. The whole scheme is absurd. I propose to vote against the appropriation of $100,000 for this purpose, and against that of $600,000 for assisted immigration to Canada until the conditions are better, and until this is a more satisfactory country for people to come to, and for the people who are now here to live in.

I had not intended taking part in this debate but in view of the manner in which some hon. members have discussed this most serious question I rise to make known my views from a humanitarian standpoint. The economic system of this country has been such that all those who own the public, utilities which the farmers and agriculturists of Canada need to use-the railways, the banks, the grain dealers, the elevator concerns and the loan companies-are accumulating great wealth, while the man who creates the new wealth of this country every year does not make enough to clothe and feed himself in decency. Some of these men are still hanging on to their farms in the hope of salvaging something out of the labour which they have bo many years devoted to the building up of what they fondly call home. Why any government should inveigle newcomers to take the places of the old and experienced farmers who have failed, without considering the reason for that failure is to my mind political insanity. The present immigration policy is nothing more than the inveigling of the uninformed into taking the places of men who, through hard times, have had to leave their farms every year. The time was when we thought that the western part of this country was rich enough to carry any overhead expense, and we built thousands of miles of railway which have never been needed and which can never economically serve the interests of Canada. Freight rates were in-

creased to pay the dividends of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. This, it was said, was needed to maintain the country's credit and the settler had to pay for it. Our legislators have looked on with unconcern whilst the lake shipping combine, and other combines obtained control of the wealth which the farmer each year made for this country. The effort was made to ease the settler's mind by telling him how much his farm had increased in value; and so he went on adding to the wealth of the country and borrowing at a high rate of interest from the banks, to meet his own obligations. Implement companies have been left to conduct their operations virtually as they pleased. So the dance has gone merrily on.
There are a good many things which the government can do in the way of carrying out a consistent immigration policy, but it seems to me that they are still surveying the situation with unconcern. The present immigration vote, under existing conditions, is certainly bound to meet with lively opposition. It is known to all that are on the land endeavouring to make a living that it is useless to bring in settlers under present conditions to take the place of experienced farmers who are failing to make good. The fact that the Acting Minister of Immigration says the present conditions are largely our own fault does not alter the case. It was not the war, as he says, that caused excessive or undue inflation of the price of land. The conditions with which we are now faced threatened to arise before the war began; the war only postponed them for a time. The conditions, coupled with the rise in freight rates, have been so bad that the farmers' products have fallen even below the prices which prevailed previous to 1914. I think it is certainly reasonable to say that under present conditions it is a useless waste to spend money on immigration. Take the case of a new settler. The proposition is to people 20,000,000 acres of land within ten or fifteen miles of the railways. Now, just see what the overhead expenses of the intending settler will be to start with, and I have only mentioned those things it is imperative for him to have. He needs a binder, which costs under present conditions $330; a drill, which costs $180; a wagon, which costs $160; a plough, which costs $60; a harrow, which costs $30; and a rake and mower, which costs $180. He will also need four horses, costing $400, and he should have two cows which he can buy at present for about $40 each. Then he should have in cash- outside of what he can make as he goes along-to feed his family for one year and a

half until returns come in, at least $600. He will also need another $100 for fuel. Now he requires to buy a quarter section at $20 per acre, and if he can get the necessary money at 6 per cent that will represent an interest charge of about $204. He has to pay the interest the first year, but at the end of the second season he still finds himself in debt $2,324. Now it seems to me that he cannot borrow this amount from the bank because the present rate of interest is too high. One of the reasons why farms are vacant to-day is that the rates of interest are so high that it [DOT] does not pay to borrow money to work a farm.
I just rose to say that I oppose the vote for this expenditure on immigration, and I do it largely from a humanitarian standpoint.

Mr. Chairman, I listened, this afternoon, with great satisfaction to the government's policy on this important question of immigration; it gave me much pleasure to hear the eloquent speech delivered by the Minister of the Interior, who gave us a masterly outline of the situation. I therefore approve of the government's policy. I am in favour of this wise moderate policy, and, I think we are fully justified, under the circumstances, to avoid extremes and more than ever we can say in medio stat virtus. No doubt the country is in need of immigration but a select and desirable one; Canada must not follow the example of other countries and hold a wide opened door to all immigrants of the world. It seems to me, that at this period in our history, it would be bad policy to erect either on our Atlantic coast or the shores of the St. Lawrence, a new Statue of Liberty opening widely its mantle to gather in all the wandering children of the earth.
I listened with pleasure to the Minister of the Interior bringing out new features in regard to this immigration policy. I think the criticism of the government by the opposition for following up the old policy is not well founded, because as I have stated there is in the government's policy new features. In fact there is the co-operation of the government wdth the provinces. This is a new element which will be appreciated by the people of this country. Another new feature is the one of the publicity which will be widespread encouraging immigration not only towards the western provinces as in the past, but towards the nine provinces of the Dominion. These are the new features introduced in the policy of immigration that deserve to be pointed out and with which I entirely agree. This new policy is acknowledged by the Progressive

New Member
party since they reproach the government for changing the old policy by introducing this special new feature by which the Dominion government would co-operate with the provinces and, they seem rather astonished at the fact of this co-operation. We may have, in the past, made mistakes- by opening too wide the gates to immigrants and especially by directing them towards those territories, the western provinces, only which, according to certain people,, seem to be well fitted to immigration.
A member of the opposition commenting upon the remarks made by a previous speaker, stated that the important questions which interested the country, at present, were those of immigration and railways, and, that both had been discussed in a masterly way by the speaker who had preceded him. No doubt these two questions are of the utmost importance; but 'to my mind, there is one which dominates both of them: it is the question of colonization. The latter holds the foremost place, while railways and immigration are but means to attain the great aim. It is by cooperating with the provinces that we may help immigration and especially colonization in this country.
No doubt in the western provinces this co-operation cannot exist between the Dominion government and the provincial government for the simple reason that the natural resources belong to the former. These provinces take no interest in the question because they cannot supply lands to those who wish to settle in this country. In the older provinces, the eastern provinces, it is absolutely necessary that lands favourable to farming be offered to settlers so as to help immigration. There must be lands offered but there must also be settlers to take them over. This work accomplished by the older provinces and that the Dominion government now wish to help, is an excellent thing for this country. Indeed, it was by opening up areas of arable lands that we were able to keep our people in this country; it is through such a colonization policy that we succeeded in preventing the exodus of our children to the United States, and it will again be through applying such a policy, backed by both Dominion and provincial governments that we shall hold the settlers amongst us and assist in the work known as repatriation. If praise is due to the government, at present, it is certainly for having contributed to establish the work of repatriation. I wish to congratulate them on this achievement, and, on having designated to perform such work a man whose ability is indisputable. Indeed, Mr. Arthur Lemont has a wide experience
in economic questions; he was attached during a number of years to the Department of Colonization in our province; as a journalist, during twenty years, he wrote on all the important subjects interesting our country and has even published works on Canadian economic questions. I have reason to hope that this organization and under the direction of the official in charge repatriation will proceed in an efficient manner.
These are the views 'that I wished to emphasize in this debate. I renew my most sincere adhesion to the government's policy. I state that we should encourage the repatriation of our people to the older provinces, and, specially my own province, and that we should also help in the settlement of the western provinces. Those who wish to return and live under the skies of their province are always welcome. At present, settlers are not numerous enough; they must come in greater numbers so as to further develop the eastern provinces. If amongst us, there are people having an adventurous turn of mind, rather than cross the 45th parallel to seek work in the New England mills, they would be better off to go west and settle the. Red river, the Assiniboine and Saskatchewan valleys, taking their place among their own people already settled in those parts, and who, thanks to Providence, are prosperous. I therefore favour this policy of the government in regard to immigration and shall cast my vote with pleasure in support of the credits asked by the government.
